<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comMon, 12 Oct 2026 19:52:07 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Investment vehicle sues over financing plan for apartment scheme in Leopardstown]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/10/12/investment-vehicle-sues-over-south-dublin-apartment-scheme-financing-plan/https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/10/12/investment-vehicle-sues-over-south-dublin-apartment-scheme-financing-plan/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 17:12:32 +0000A corporate investment vehicle set up to acquire a residential site in south Dublin is suing a company over alleged misrepresentation as to projected returns and non-disclosure of an aggregate promoter fee.

Merleview Ltd has brought Commercial Court proceedings against Burton Carman Ltd, a special purpose vehicle set up to acquire, hold and develop a property at Leopardstown Park with a view, it is claimed, to develop around 145 build-to-rent apartments. It is also suing Elkstone Capital Partners Ltd, which was the promoter and manager of the investment in Burton Carman.

The defendants deny the claims.

The case was entered to the fast track Commercial Court on Monday by Judge Eileen Roberts on consent between the parties.

It was adjourned to next month after the judge was told there may be mediation or alternatively, the defendants say, the dispute may be covered by an arbitration clause.

In a sworn statement seeking entry of the case to the commercial list, Andrew Murphy, a director of Merleview, said that in February 2022, Elkstone director and chief revenue officer Ruairí O’Neill presented him with an “equity opportunity pitch deck” and a “debt opportunity pitch deck” concerning the development of the Leopardstown property. It was proposed to develop it as a private rental sector scheme of around 145 apartments.

Murphy said the pitch decks forecast an exit value of €14.9 million, an equity return of 42 per cent IRR (internal rate of return) and a 2.01 times multiple on a €2.9 million equity investment over 24 months along with a senior debt coupon of 10 per cent a year.

On the strength of these representations, Murphy said, Merleview subscribed for ordinary shares in Burton Carman and advanced an accompanying senior debt facility, together totalling €446,969.

In July 2023, Merleview advanced a further amount of some €303,000 as a loan note.

Murphy said the executed loan note certificate stated an interest rate of 7.5 per cent per annum even though the “debt deck”, and O’Neill’s own representations, had put the rate at 10 per cent.

In August, the defendants’ solicitors sent a corrected certificate showing an interest rate of 10 per cent on the loan note from March 2023 and acknowledging the original cert had been wrong in relation to that.

In April 2026, Merleview raised 10 categories of complaint against Elkstone including misrepresentation as to projected returns and the interest rate and non-disclosure of an aggregate promoter fee entitlement of some €781,000, which Murphy said was equivalent to 15.5 per cent of the total capital raised of some €5 million.

There was also an unauthorised material change to the investment strategy from a private rental sector scheme to a build-to-sell scheme without the investor majority consent required, Murphy said.

There was also a breach of ongoing reporting obligations under the subscription and shareholders agreement (SSA), he added.

The defendants’ solicitors denied liability and that Elkstone owed Merleview no duty of care given the disclaimers in the pitch decks and the SSA.

Merleview issued proceedings last August claiming recovery of the €303,000 principal sum under the loan note, damages for breach of duty, and for intentional interference with Merleview’s economic interests.

Murphy said it was important the proceedings be resolved without delay as Merleview’s senior debt and loan notes have been in default since July 2025 and no principal has been repaid to date. Interest continues to accrue, he said.

Despite repeated requests, he said, the defendants have not produced audited accounts, management reports or verified fee accounts and the parties are in dispute as to Merleview’s entitlement under the SSA to withhold consent to certain proposed transactions pending provision of the information.

The defendants’ solicitors have also indicated an intention to apply for security for costs against Merleview. However, Merleview says it is a fully solvent company.

]]>w-ings<![CDATA[Sky Ireland revenue rises with help from Rory McIlroy 2025 Masters win]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/skys-irish-revenues-rise-helped-by-rory-mcilroys-masters-win/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/skys-irish-revenues-rise-helped-by-rory-mcilroys-masters-win/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 16:12:16 +0000Rory McIlroy’s winning putt in the 2025 Masters at Augusta last year helped the Irish arm of Sky to increase revenue by 7 per cent to £539 million (€637 million).

The revenue increase was also helped by Sky Ireland imposing a 4.5 per cent price hike on average for Sky customers here.

Sky Broadband has now delivered more than 50 consecutive quarters of customer growth.

Earlier this year, in its battle against the piracy of Sky channels through so-called dodgy boxes, the company issued about 200 cease-and-desist letters to individuals.

Details of 300 ‘dodgy box’ users to be provided to Sky, High Court hears

The vast majority of the individuals who were served letters are in Co Wexford and it is understood that the compliance level has been high on receipt of the letters.

A spokesman for Sky Ireland said today: “Sky invests significantly in protecting our content, which can include taking action against those who watch Sky without paying the proper subscription fee.

“For those individuals who received cease-and-desist letters earlier in the year, who did not return undertakings, we are moving towards further action. This may include, where necessary, seeking court injunctions to prevent continued use of illegal IPTV services and pursuing damages for copyright infringement and legal costs.”

]]>Richard Heathcote<![CDATA[Aviva expands flood insurance access to 13,000 properties following ‘granular’ map update]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/aviva-expands-flood-insurance-access-to-13000-properties-following-granular-map-update/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/aviva-expands-flood-insurance-access-to-13000-properties-following-granular-map-update/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 17:44:20 +0000Aviva has increased access to flood protection insurance for an additional 13,000 homes and businesses across the State following reforms to its “extremely granular” flood risk map, the insurer said.

The enhancement comes two months after the Government established its Flood Insurance Protection Gap Working Group, of which Aviva, one of the largest general insurance providers in the Irish market, is a member.

This move “is a positive example of the progress being made through investment in flood protection measures, improved understanding of risk and greater collaboration across stakeholders,” said Joanie Hughes, managing director of personal lines at Aviva.

Julie Frazer, head of product, underwriting and intermediary within the personal lines division, said Aviva was “constantly updating its risk assessments” and “regularly reviews data” to do with flood risk.

She said recent “severe weather events”, such as Storm Chandra and Storm Eowyn, “absolutely inform our decisions” on the matter.

The insurer has since updated its “extremely granular maps ... based on the probability of a flood event occurring” at any given property, she said.

The 13,000 additional properties are “very much widespread right across the country.

“Flood risk can be really localised”, with the rock type, hill incline, and proximity to a body of water all factors that can result in “one property being able to access flood protection and another one ‘just up the road’ not,” Frazer continued.

ESB battens down the hatches for storm season

“Needless to say, the flood protection gap is something we’re very conscious of and would like to help to close,” she went on, “it’s very much at the forefront of our minds.”

Market research conducted by 3Gem Research & Insights on behalf of Aviva “reveals growing awareness among homeowners of the risks posed by extreme weather”, the insurer said.

While it found one-in-10 homeowners have experienced flood damage in the past five years, 24 per cent have experienced “storm-related damage”, and 62 per cent are “concerned” of extreme-weather damage over the next five years.

“Despite high levels of awareness and concern, almost half of homeowners (46 per cent) have not made any improvements to protect their property from extreme weather over the past two years,” Aviva said.

Common actions taken include upgrading gutter systems, repairing roofs, purchasing emergency kits and improving drainage systems, the research of 1,000 homeowners found.

Aviva advised homeowners to inform themselves of weather warnings and local flood risks through alerts from Met Éireann and to consider implementing “practical reliance measures” such as flood barriers to their properties.

The Government established in August a flood insurance working group. Tánaiste Simon Harris said “it will bring together the key public and private sector stakeholders needed to identify practical solutions to one of the most challenging issues facing the insurance market”.

“We have been very much involved with this alongside all of our peers in the industry,” Frazer said. “We’re very determined to find a way to deal with the flood protection gap – we understand and appreciate the difficulties it can create for homeowners and business owners,” she said.

]]>Leah Farrell<![CDATA[European stocks rise with banks proving a safe bet]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/european-stocks-rise-with-banks-proving-a-safe-bet/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/european-stocks-rise-with-banks-proving-a-safe-bet/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 17:07:31 +0000Stocks across Europe largely rose on Monday, bolstered by investor confidence in the banking sectors and strong returns by drinks and luxury giants.

Close to home, banking also proved a safe investment as Dublin’s stock market saw positive returns from financial groups, manufacturers and construction companies alike.

Across the Atlantic, however, many traders were hesitant to begin the week with a strong start as key inflation data looms later in the week, seen to be pivotal in shaping the Federal Reserve’s economic forecasts and the trajectory of interest rates.

DUBLIN

The Iseq All-Share index rose 1.60 per cent to start the week in the green, closing at 14,123.87 following positive results in the banking and manufacturing sectors.

Strong gains by the building materials and insulation manufacturer Kingspan, whose share price rose 2.41 per cent to €101.80 by close of business, were among the day’s top results.

Elsewhere, home builder Glenveagh Properties was up 1.77 per cent to close at €2.30 a share, while Cairn Homes grew by 0.03 per cent to close at €2.64. Food technology company Kerry Group also saw strong returns, up 1.45 per cent at €88.70 a share.

Both major banks traded on the index saw their share price increase. Bank of Ireland was up 1.79 per cent to close at €18.46, while rival AIB lagged slightly behind, up 1.68 per cent to finish at €10.86.

Agri-services group Origin Enterprises and healthcare company Uniphar also saw their share prices increase, 3.95 per cent and 3.26 per cent to €3.95 and €3.97 a share, respectively.

Insurer FBD Holdings saw its share price drop, down 1.84 per cent to €18.65 by the end of the trading day.

LONDON

The London stock market saw stocks largely rise across the board, with its blue-chip FTSE 100 index increasing 0.99 per cent and the mid-cap FTSE 250 up 0.47 per cent as well.

Investors put their trust in British banks, with Lloyds Banking Group rising 2.36 per cent and Barclays not far behind, up 1.85 per cent by close. Meanwhile, Lion Finance also jumped 2.75 per cent.

Guinness-brewer Diageo, who also owns Smirnoff Vodka and Don Julio tequila, ended the day up 2.14 per cent on Friday’s closing price.

Telecommunications group Vodafone, however, dipped 1.39 per cent by close – as did publishing and exhibitions group Informa, whose share price fell 2.41 per cent.

EUROPE

Elsewhere in Europe, investors in banking portfolios and luxury goods suppliers helped the continent’s two major indices also close the trading day with growth.

The Stoxx 600 index was up 0.65 per cent, while the Stoxx 50 followed, up 0.45.

Spain’s Santander bank increased 1.80 per cent, while German Deutsche Telekom rose 1.13 per cent.

Elsewhere, France’s luxury good giant Hermes International soared 2.10 per cent by close. Car manufacturer Mercedes Benz Group, however, saw its share price dip 0.82 per cent.

NEW YORK

Early trades on Wall Street pointed to a slightly less positive trend compared with global indices.

Some stocks fluctuated near their all-time highs while others faltered as traders looked ahead to the start of the earnings season.

Before midday New York time, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 0.43 per cent, meanwhile the S&P saw little change and the Nasdaq fell some 0.60 per cent.

Most companies in the S&P 500 rose despite renewed losses in chipmakers and looming inflation data to be released later this week that will be key in shaping the Federal Reserve’s outlook. – Additional reporting: Bloomberg.

]]><![CDATA[Supreme Court rejects application to appeal plan for data centre in Ennis]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/supreme-court-rejects-application-to-appeal-plan-for-data-centre-in-ennis/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/supreme-court-rejects-application-to-appeal-plan-for-data-centre-in-ennis/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 15:24:32 +0000

The Supreme Court has dismissed an application by opponents of a 200MW €1.6 billion data centre on the outskirts of Ennis for leave to appeal against a High Court decision, clearing all legal hurdles faced by the project.

In its determination, the Supreme Court has dismissed the three grounds put forward in the application by opponents of the data centre, namely Colin Doyle, Friends of the Irish Environment CLG, Futureproof Clare, Martin Knox and Christine Sharp.

The Supreme Court found the application did not meet the constitutional threshold required for leave to be granted to appeal the High Court upholding the planning permission granted by An Coimisiún Pleanála (ACP) to Art Data Centres Ltd.

In its determination, the Supreme Court found that “no point of general public importance arises” in the grounds put forward by the appellants.

ACP granted planning permission in April 2024 to Art Data Centres Ltd comprising six data halls covering 145 acres or 1.3 million sq ft on lands adjacent to the Tulla Road on the eastern outskirts of Ennis near Junction 13 on the M18 motorway connecting Galway to Limerick.

The project is set to generate up to 1,200 jobs during construction, and up to a 1,000 permanent jobs and the underpinning of thousands more in digital industries.

On Monday, the joint founders of Art Data Centres, Tom McNamara and Vincent Fogarty, said the ruling “recognises that there is a future for environmentally-sensitive data centre developments like ours, where there is responsible use of renewable energy, grid-supporting generation technology and heat-recycling for both agri-food and local heating schemes”.

They described the Supreme Court ruling as “great news for this data centre campus and for Clare as the project will be a key pillar of the Ennis 2040 Economic Plan for the area”.

The project’s 200MW scale “will be attractive to the largest technology partners in the world and the project represents the culmination of more than ten years of preparatory work”, they said.

They said the connection applications could be finally processed following the Supreme Court ruling “and work will commence in 2027 as soon as all is in place”.

]]><![CDATA[Takeover panel rejects PTSB sale complaints from ex-banker ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/financial-services/2026/10/12/takeover-panel-rejects-ptsb-sale-complaints-from-ex-banker/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/financial-services/2026/10/12/takeover-panel-rejects-ptsb-sale-complaints-from-ex-banker/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 09:48:30 +0000The Irish Takeover Panel has rejected concerns raised about the PTSB sale process from a firm cofounded by boom-time Irish banker Mark Duffy, which has also indicated it is considering an 11th-hour bid for the bank.

Axis Capital, an advisory business cofounded by former Bank of Scotland (Ireland) chief executive Duffy, sent a letter to the panel on July 27th that consolidated “a number of matters” it had previously raised in relation to the proposed €1.62 billion acquisition of PTSB by Austrian banking group Bawag.

The panel said that “having carefully considered the substance of all of the matters raised by Axis”, it has ruled there was no case laid out that amounted to any breach of Irish takeover rules.

The announcement comes just weeks before the High Court, which is overseeing the so-called scheme-of-arrangement deal for PTSB to be sold to Bawag, is due to hold its sanctioning hearing on October 27th.

Axis made an intervention on October 2nd saying it was considering making a bid for PTSB. Last Friday, a long-term dissenting PTSB shareholder, Scotchstone Capital, led by Piotr Skoczylas, also said it was weighing a bid for PTSB. Neither has confirmed whether it has secured any funding for a bid.

Axis is being advised by Quirin Privatbank in Berlin and law firm Belmont Legal in Frankfurt.

Axis helped initiate talks in 2025 between New York private equity firm Centerbridge, the Department of Finance and PTSB over a potential deal for the Irish bank. The US group subsequently submitted a non-binding proposal in September last year for the State’s 57.5 per cent stake in the bank.

Centerbridge was the underbidder to Bawag in April as a formal sales process, initiated in October, concluded.

Axis was reported by the Business Post in July to have been urging minority shareholders to vote against the planned Bawag deal at an extraordinary general meeting (egm) later that month. Axis said in a note circulated to shareholders it had become “increasingly uncomfortable with the way the process has developed”, claiming there had been “inordinate involvement from one shareholder, leaving others effectively as bystanders”.

In July, Duffy said in a post on LinkedIn, the professional social networking platform, that the panel should reopen the sale process to allow “all credible bidders to make their best and final bids to all shareholders”.

PTSB secured backing from 91.3 per cent of shareholders – led by the Government – for the Bawag takeover at the July egm. However, some 36 per cent of minority investors voted against the transaction at the meeting.

It is expected the High Court will be asked by some minority shareholders to order the holding of a separate vote of minority investors. PTSB has repeatedly said it had “very strong” legal advice that only one vote was necessary.

]]><![CDATA[DAA says staff in Saudi Arabia ‘safe and well’ after latest airport attacks]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/daa-says-staff-in-saudi-arabia-safe-and-well-after-latest-airport-attacks/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/daa-says-staff-in-saudi-arabia-safe-and-well-after-latest-airport-attacks/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 13:28:32 +0000Dublin Airport operator DAA has said that all of its staff in Saudi Arabia are “safe and well” after Yemen’s Houthi forces launched more attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh in recent days.

An attack on the airport on Saturday, the third in a week, killed 12 people and wounded more than 300, part of a tit-for-tat military escalation by the Houthis against the Saudis.

Separately, an unidentified projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport on Sunday, with authorities tackling a blaze, the Saudi-led coalition said in a statement.

In a statement on Monday, a spokesman for DAA said: “We are aware of the incidents at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh over the weekend and can confirm that all our team members in the region are safe and well. DAA declined to say how many staff it has in Saudi Arabia due to commercial sensitivities and security considerations.

The blast at the Riyadh airport on Saturday brought travel to a near-standstill. It also forced the capital’s financial hub to shift to remote work until further notice and prompted executives from BP and Shell to pull out of a big energy event in the city this week.

The Department of Foreign Affairs “strongly advises Irish citizens against all but essential travel to Saudi Arabia until further notice” due to the security situation in the Middle East and Gulf.

Irish citizens already in the region are advised to avoid “unnecessary journeys, remain vigilant, closely monitor developments and local media, and follow the advice of local authorities”.

Saturday’s strike came less than a week after Saudi-backed forces in Yemen launched a campaign to retake Houthi-held areas and “eliminate” the group. The militants, who frequently claim attacks on Saudi oil facilities, had recently seized more Yemeni territory and bolstered their control over the Bab el-Mandeb, a global shipping chokepoint.

The Saudi-led coalition called “the cowardly terrorist attack” on the airport on Saturday “a full-fledged war crime” by the Houthis.

The victims included four Saudis, a Palestinian, two Bangladeshis and one person each from the US, Egypt, Jordan, Syria and Sudan, according to authorities. – Additional reporting: Bloomberg

]]>AP<![CDATA[Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: Here’s how the scheme will work]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/06/consumers-can-save-up-to-50000-tax-free-in-new-personal-investment-accounts/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/06/consumers-can-save-up-to-50000-tax-free-in-new-personal-investment-accounts/Tue, 06 Oct 2026 15:44:46 +0000People will be able to put €12,000 a year tax-free into the Government new personal investment accounts, Minister for Finance Simon Harris announced in his Budget 2027 speech.

The accounts will feature a low tax rate of just 1 per cent. However, this tax will be levied on any amount in the account over a tax-free threshold of €50,000, not just the profit the account made over that year.

This holds out the prospect of people paying tax on their savings in years when they lost money simply because the balance of their account was above the €50,000 tax-free threshold.

Harris said the new accounts will be available from July 1st next year. About €170 billion is currently on deposit in Irish bank accounts, with the Minister having previously described that money as “sitting idle”.

Alongside the new accounts, the Minister announced a financial literacy campaign. The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) has set up a webpage that will allow people to read up about issues around investing, and the choices available.

It also offers a quick multiple choice self-assessment quiz that allows consumers to assess their investment readiness.

Irish households hold just 2.3 per cent of their financial assets in direct investments such as listed shares and debt securities, compared with an EU average of approximately 7.5 per cent.

Budget Q&A: Submit your questions to our expert panel on budget day

The new scheme has been designed to encourage people to move their savings into market investments.

“The long-mooted investment account is an important step towards making long-term investment more accessible,” said Cróna Clohisey, director of members and advocacy at Chartered Accountants Ireland. “Now that the broad design has been announced, Government should move quickly to finalise the legislation, systems and guidance so that financial service providers can establish these accounts and people can begin using them.

“It is critical that there is no delay to the introduction timeline of mid-2027,” she said.

Michael Healy, chief executive of IG Consumer, said the Government had missed the chance to get Irish people investing.

“While the decision to set the tax-free threshold at €50,000 is better than we expected, it is a small victory within a fundamentally flawed model. The €12,000 annual contribution limit is far too low if the ambition is to get people investing seriously and building meaningful long-term wealth.

“But the bigger problem is the proposed 1 per cent annual tax on investments above the threshold,” said Healy. “Taxing the value of an investment rather than the return it generates means someone could face a tax bill even when their investments have fallen in value – effectively paying tax on losses. That is the wrong principle for an account designed to encourage people to invest.”

Budget Calculator 2027: Here’s how this year’s budget will affect your income

Robert Dever, head of tax at Eversheds Sutherland, agreed. The Government he said had adopted a cautious approach to the new scheme. “For a lot of taxpayers, in the long term, it will probably be more tax efficient to maximise tax relief arising on pension contributions before contributing to an investment account.”

However, Rory O’Brien, head of wealth management, Dublin, at Baker Tilly Ireland Wealth was more upbeat.

“On the whole, the new Irish Investment Account looks like a fantastic opportunity for those looking for better returns from the investment markets over the medium to long term to do so without being harshly punished when their investments do well. The opportunity for younger investors to start small and build up to the 50k without CGT is very positive and l would expect those looking to build deposits, to consider this as a viable option.”

The Government also announced a lowering of the rate of tax under the “deemed disposal” or exit tax regime that applies to investors in products currently available in the market.

Budget 2027 main points: Minimum wage to rise 79 cent; €12,000 per year limit for investment scheme

Last year, as part of Budget 2026, the deemed disposal tax rate was reduced from 41 per cent to 38 per cent. In 2024, a report by the Department of Finance into the funds sector advised the deemed disposal rule should be ended for exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and investment funds.

Exit tax is levied on profits when an investment is cashed in. Deemed disposal sees that tax levied every eight years after an investment is taken out, even if the investment is not cashed in.

Chartered Accountants Ireland’s Cróna Clohisey said it was “extremely disheartening that the eight-year deemed disposal rule remains. It has no place in a modern Irish investment landscape.

“Requiring people to pay tax on gains they have not realised undermines the benefits of long-term investment, adds unnecessary complexity for individual investors, and contradicts the wider Government drive to foster retail investment and encourage greater financial literacy.”

Irish Funds chairwoman, Andrea Kelly welcome dthe three point cut in the rate of tax but said the lack of any clear path to phasing out deemed disposal was “deeply disappointing”.

“The Government should now use the Finance Bill to provide the certainty that was missing from the Budget,” she said.

New accounts

Anyone over the age of 18 who is resident in the State and holds a PPS number can invest in the new personal investment scheme, but they can only have one account.

Eligible investments will include listed shares, listed bonds, financial instruments traded on a regulated market and a range of investment funds suitable for retail investors, including ETFs.

Investors will not be permitted to invest in what are deemed highly complex and risky products, including derivatives and crypto assets.

Catch up with all your Budget 2027 news here

There will be no minimum holding or lock-in period, and moving investment accounts between providers will be allowed, where possible, on a tax-neutral basis.

Any tax due will be calculated and paid at source by the companies providing the investment funds available under the scheme.

What is not yet clear is how much providers will charge for the products they offer.

Harris first announced his intention to introduce a new form of consumer-friendly investment account back in February.

He has returned to the theme regularly since then but, until Tuesday, had declined to confirm the amount that could be put into such accounts each month or year, the threshold above which the funds will be taxed, or the rate of taxation.

Harris’s department had examined similar types of accounts operating in other countries. Ultimately, it opted largely for the Swedish model despite strong industry lobbying in favour of the rival UK individual savings account (ISA) model.

]]><![CDATA[AI being used by employers to more closely monitor their staff, Dublin conference hears]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/12/employers-use-ai-to-monitor-staff-who-also-dont-benefit-from-the-tech-conference-hears/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/12/employers-use-ai-to-monitor-staff-who-also-dont-benefit-from-the-tech-conference-hears/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 07:00:00 +0000Artificial intelligence (AI) is being used by employers to more closely monitor their staff to make them more productive, a trade union organised conference in Dublin has heard.

Some will be irked by that charge, especially in years where stock markets have fallen. However, a UK-style tax-free wrapper, allowing savers to invest up to £20,000 a year completely free of tax, always appeared excessively generous and politically indefensible.

For the Government, a Swedish-type approach offers a predictable tax stream while encouraging people to put their savings into shares and funds (and a €50,000 tax-free limit is more generous than many expected) rather than leaving them in cash.

The Government says it intends to move beyond deemed disposal during the lifetime of this administration, but substantive reform has again been deferred.

And there is a second, less discussed problem. The Funds Sector 2030 review recommended limited loss relief, but the Government’s roadmap says it will not be introduced. Some will have issues with the SIA, but it’s arguably a welcome attempt to make investing simpler. The harder task is making the wider investing tax system equally sensible.

]]><![CDATA[A good night’s sleep is a class issue]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/11/a-good-nights-sleep-is-a-class-issue/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/11/a-good-nights-sleep-is-a-class-issue/Sun, 11 Oct 2026 09:00:00 +0000In the 1920s, a pair of sociologists set out to study “the interwoven trends that are the life of a small American city” at a time of rapid change.

In their subsequent book about Muncie, Indiana (which they anonymised as “Middletown”), they wrote that the community was divided by time as well as class.

At 6am, the lights were going on in working-class households because their jobs generally began between 6.15 and 7.30am (when they weren’t on night shifts), while the “business class” households remained slumbering until later.

These different working rhythms became political in 1925 when a deadlock emerged over whether the city should adopt “daylight saving time”, which would mean longer light on summer evenings.

The working-class early risers argued they would lose sleep, while the businessmen urged the change “because of golf” and the need to deal with businesses on the east coast.

The competing demands for leisure and business on the one hand, and of our body clocks on the other, have not gone away over the ensuing century. But scientists have learned a lot more about what happens to our health when we prioritise the former over the latter.

In short: nothing good. Many researchers now agree that daylight saving time can interfere with our circadian rhythms. But there are much more dangerous ways to meddle with our biological clocks, the worst of which is to work at night.

It is a myth that night-shift workers can become nocturnal over time. According to the book Life Time by professor of circadian neuroscience Russell Foster, studies suggest that 97 per cent of night shift workers remain synchronised to daytime, which means they have to sleep when their bodies are primed to be awake, and vice versa.

There are consequences for blood pressure and the immune system. The correlations with cancer are so clear that night work has been classed as “probably carcinogenic to humans” by the World Health Organisation’s International Agency for Research on Cancer.

Maynooth-led sleep research will examine links with mental health

Even if you don’t work overnight, evidence suggests that just working against your “chronotype” can be bad for your health. One recent study from Finland looked at what happened to people who gave information about whether they were morning people or “night owls” in 2012 when they were in their mid-40s.

Over the following 12 years, those with evening chronotypes were more likely to end up on disability pensions, even after adjusting for socio-economic factors. One possibility, according to the researchers, is that “traditional working times interfere significantly with the sleeping preferences of late chronotypes, leading to social jet lag”.

But while the prevalence of night work has declined gradually in the US since Middletown was written, there is still a class divide when it comes to work that tramples over your body clock. According to research published this year, most US night workers have no more than a high-school education.

More broadly, the pandemic-induced shift towards remote work has been a bigger boon for white-collar workers (who already had more flexibility over their hours) than anyone else.

What ‘smart’ watches get wrong and right when tracking the quality of your sleep

In Europe, for example, managers have the highest levels of autonomy according to 2024’s vast European Working Conditions Survey, with 40 per cent able to adapt their working hours within certain limits, and 19 per cent having full control over their schedules. In contrast, workers at the bottom end of the pay scale continue to have little control: nearly 80 per cent have schedules set entirely by their employers.

It is possible that advances in automation will eventually do away with the need for humans to work against their body clocks. Already, some logistics companies are beginning to experiment with “lights-out night shifts” in which robots work overnight alone, setting aside those orders that require human assistance until the morning shift arrives.

Self-driving trucks, meanwhile, could cover long highway stretches overnight, saving the “final mile deliveries” for human drivers to do in daytime.

Such a transition would be economically challenging for workers – not least since night-shift work usually pays a premium – but could have huge benefits for human health. It would require careful navigation by policymakers with an eye on science, inequality and the future.

Yet US president Donald Trump sounds much more like a voice from the past. His latest intervention into the “politics of time” is to push for daylight saving time to be made permanent, arguing that it would be good for people who would “like to play golf a little bit without having to run home after 14 holes”. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

]]>Frank Miller<![CDATA[AI bubble? Nvidia is now bigger than Japan, but valuation looks modest]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/11/ai-bubble-nvidia-is-now-bigger-than-japan-but-valuation-looks-modest/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/11/ai-bubble-nvidia-is-now-bigger-than-japan-but-valuation-looks-modest/Sun, 11 Oct 2026 05:56:00 +0000It has been a long four months for Nvidia shareholders. The world’s most valuable company has finally set a new record high, ending a 96-trading-day drought.

Of course, a 96-day wait would be unremarkable by the standards of most companies, but Nvidia is another matter, with Bespoke Investment noting this was shareholders’ third-longest wait since ChatGPT’s November 2022 launch.

The four-month lull is easier to put in perspective when the numbers – Nvidia was worth $5.8 trillion at its recent peak – are considered. Comparisons between Nvidia and entire national stock markets have become routine, but Japan was the one big exception.

No longer – Nvidia now accounts for 5.2 per cent of the MSCI All Country World Index, slightly more than Japan and more than every country except the US.

Taiwan (3.5 per cent), the UK and Canada (2.9 per cent each) trail well behind, while Nvidia’s weighting is almost three times that of Germany’s.

A casual observer might think this screams AI bubble, but Nvidia is not an obviously expensive stock. It trades on about 15 times estimated earnings, according to market data from Finviz, making it cheaper than 295 of the S&P 500’s component stocks.

The company, too, is acting as if shares are reasonably priced. A fortnight ago, Nvidia authorised an additional $150 billion share buyback, the largest such authorisation in history.

The record-breaking numbers make for an odd combination, with Nvidia simultaneously looking enormous enough to distort global equity indices, whilst remaining relatively inexpensive against the earnings it is producing.

]]>Heather Diehl<![CDATA[Tesco dines out on customers staying in to cook its Finest range]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/10/tesco-gets-to-dine-out-on-customers-staying-in-to-cook-its-finest-range/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/10/tesco-gets-to-dine-out-on-customers-staying-in-to-cook-its-finest-range/Sun, 11 Oct 2026 04:58:00 +0000The finals of the World Steak Challenge in Amsterdam didn’t escape the eye of Cantillon in recent weeks.

Two Irish entries made it into the winners’ enclosure, with cuts from the country taking home the prizes for world’s best grass-fed ribeye and sirloin.

The winners were Lidl Ireland and Tesco Ireland. Tesco followed up the steak win by going on to claim 86 prizes at the Blas na hÉireann Irish Food Awards.

The UK supermarket chain, led by Irish man Ken Murphy, has sought out these industry awards as seals of approval for its Finest range as it bids to push premium.

Consumer sentiment and spending data would imply it’s a curious time for the supermarket to be pushing its premium own-label range.

Irish shoppers are well aware they have been forced to suck up sustained increases to their weekly shop in recent years, with their annual bill up about €3,000 since 2021.

Last month, when polling showed cost-of-living pressures dominated voters’ priorities ahead of Budget 2027, the latest figures from Worldpanel by Numerator showed grocery inflation was up 4.3 per cent. If a household was spending €200 a week on groceries, that would add close to €450 to their annual bill.

More recent data this week from the Central Statistics Office showed Irish consumer prices were up 4.1 per cent year on year in September, which was the fastest annual rate of increase since January 2024.

Amid these cost pressures, Tesco has focused on upselling premium. Or downselling dining out, depending on how you look at it.

The company’s recent annual report said the rising cost of dining out has “resulted in a shift towards eating in and a higher demand for restaurant-quality food at home”.

If would-be diners are thinking twice about going out for their steak, they will want something to fill that void. Tesco thinks, why not our steak?

Results by the company this week suggest its bet on premium is paying off. After launching 750 new Finest products in the past year, sales of its premium range were up 12.8 per cent in Ireland.

Tesco chief financial officer Imran Nawaz was buoyed by the Irish numbers. In a call with investors, he singled out the growth in Ireland as an “exceptional performance”. A result to dine out on.

Four men have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders.

The accused – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – can be named only as Oleksandr H., Stepan K., Vitalii K. and Pavlo T. under Polish privacy law and their trial is taking place behind closed doors for security reasons.

Polish prosecutors say that they were part of an organised group tasked with “committing acts of sabotage and terrorism” on behalf of Russia’s foreign intelligence service in April and May 2024.

Those included a fire that burned down Warsaw’s largest shopping centre, Marywilska 44; another at a store in Warsaw belonging to home improvement chain OBI; and a third at an IKEA store in Vilnius. They also allegedly planned an arson attack on an IKEA store in the Latvian capital of Riga.

W Sądzie Okręgowym Warszawa-Praga ruszył proces grupy przestępczej, która miała na zlecenie Federacji Rosyjskiej podpalać markety wielkopowierzchniowe, w tym centrum handlowe przy Marywilskiej w Warszawie.https://t.co/0CFl1RyJvq

— TVN Warszawa (@tvnwarszawa) October 12, 2026

According to an indictment issued against the men in March this year, Stepan K., the Belarusian, set fire to the OBI store. Oleksandr H. is accused of involvement in the arson attack on the IKEA store in Vilnius and preparations for further attacks.

The pair have been indicted under Poland’s espionage law for carrying out acts of sabotage and terrorism on behalf of foreign intelligence. That crime carries a minimum sentence of 10 years in prison, ranging up to life.

Another Ukrainian suspect, Daniil B., had also been due to stand trial today on the same charge, with prosecutors finding that he had received an order from a handler in Russia to go to Marywilska on the night the arson attack took place and record footage of the fire and the response of the emergency services.

However, Daniil B. was jailed in Lithuania last year for his role in the Vilnius IKEA fire and Poland has not yet managed to secure his extradition for the trial in Warsaw, meaning that it went ahead without his involvement.

Polish prosecutors say they have determined that the Marywilska fire was also carried out on the orders of Russian intelligence, but have not been able to identify which individuals actually perpetrated the attack.

 

Stepan K. and Oleksandr H. – as well as Vitalii K., whom prosecutors accuse of helping carry out the arson in Vilnius – are additionally charged with participating in an organised criminal group that aimed to carry out terrorist offences, a crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison.

Both Vitalii K. and Pavlo T. were also indicted in relation to an assault in the village of Wólka Kosowska, just outside Warsaw.

Pavlo T. was already convicted in Poland last year along with two other Ukrainian men, Serhii R. and Vladyslav Y., over their role in the same criminal group tasked with carrying out acts of sabotage and terrorism by Russia. They were handed jail terms ranging from 16 months to five and a half years.

Two other alleged members of the group, Serhii Chalyi and Oleksandr Varyvoda, who prosecutors say were involved in coordinating sabotage activities, remain wanted.

Three Ukrainians have been jailed in Poland for their role in a group tasked with carrying out sabotage and terrorism.

That included the fire that destroyed Warsaw’s largest shopping centre, which Polish prosecutors say was carried out on Russia’s orders https://t.co/xuFx5T4HH9

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 24, 2025

In response to evidence that Moscow was behind the Marywilska fire, Poland last year ordered Russia’s consulate in Kraków to close. It has since closed all Russian consulates due to Moscow’s ongoing campaign of sabotage, with Russia responding by shutting down all Polish consulates on its territory.

A report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published earlier this year found that Poland is the “primary focus” of Russian sabotage in Europe.

Most recently, Poland has accused Moscow of being behind a fire at a drone factory that supplies the Polish and Ukrainian militaries. Last year, Ukrainian operatives working on behalf of Russia also used explosives in an attempt to derail a train in Poland.

Most acts of sabotage ordered by Russia in Poland have been carried out not by Russians themselves, but by Ukrainians and Belarusians, large numbers of whom already live in Poland and other countries in the region.

]]> Israeli producer had access to data harvested by Poland using Pegasus spyware, say prosecutors https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/12/israeli-producer-had-access-to-data-harvested-by-poland-using-pegasus-spyware-say-prosecutors/ Mon, 12 Oct 2026 12:27:25 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105380

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

Data harvested from mobile phones by the Polish authorities using Pegasus spyware were transmitted outside Poland and were accessible to the tool’s Israeli producer, Polish prosecutors have revealed as part of an investigation into the use of Pegasus under the former government.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk says that the case is “one of the biggest scandals in Polish history since the fall of communism”, and that it is “beyond any doubt” that the Israeli firm behind Pegasus, NSO Group, cooperates with Israeli intelligence.

Tego o Pegasusie jeszcze nie słyszeliście. pic.twitter.com/etvhTE9EWa

— Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 12, 2026

Pegasus is a powerful and controversial tool that allows the extraction of large amounts of data from mobile phones without users’ knowledge. A number of countries have been found to have used it to spy on opposition figures.

In 2017, Poland, under the government of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, purchased Pegasus from NSO. The spyware was subsequently used against hundreds of targets, including a number of PiS’s political opponents.

Among them was the head of the 2019 election campaign of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party (which was then known as Civic Platform, PO). Last year, Tusk revealed that his own wife and daughter had been among those caught up in the surveillance.

PiS, however, has insisted that Pegasus was a necessary tool to fight crime and ensure national security. It says the spyware was only used with court approval against targets legitimately suspected of wrongdoing.

 

After a coalition led by Tusk took power from PiS in December 2023, it launched investigations into the use of Pegasus under the former government.

Today, the National Prosecutor’s Office released its latest findings, based on analysis by experts at the forensic research office of Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW).

The experts confirmed that Pegasus allowed the harvesting of emails, instant messaging and text messages; the content of telephone conversations, both via mobile networks and internet calls; browsing histories, calendars and contact lists; photos, videos and other files; and location data.

“Additionally, Pegasus allowed the use of the device’s built-in microphone and cameras to record audio and video in real time and take screenshots,” reports the National Prosecutor’s Office.

Czy to możliwe, że państwo traci kontrolę nad własnym systemem inwigilacji? I to nie była stara konsola…

Z opinii biegłych ABW wynika, że CBA kupiło narzędzie, nad którym nie miało pełnej kontroli. Dane opuszczały Polskę, moduł infekujący kontrolował producent, a zagraniczna…

— Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) October 12, 2026

The ABW experts also highlighted serious concerns over management and security of the harvested data, noting that Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA), which was responsible for using the spyware, “did not have full control over the Pegasus system”.

“The CBA did not have passwords to access some accounts with administrative privileges and some system components remained under the control of the manufacturer [NSO],” wrote the prosecutor’s office. “The server module responsible for infecting mobile devices remained under the manufacturer’s exclusive control.”

Data transmitted through the Pegasus system travelled outside Polish territory, through “servers located in various parts of the world”, in a network managed by NSO and “beyond the CBA’s control”, found the experts.

Meanwhile, NSO “had technical access to materials from operational surveillance”, although prosecutors say that the experts “did not determine whether the manufacturer actually obtained access to materials from specific operations”.

The former deputy head of Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau has been charged with unlawfully sharing material obtained through surveillance using Pegasus spyware, including communication involving PM @donaldtusk's daughter when Tusk was in opposition https://t.co/LyTuqbq0KQ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 23, 2025

In a video commenting on the latest findings, Tusk said that the investigation into Pegasus was “coming to a head”. He called it “one of the biggest scandals in Polish history after the fall of communism”.

The former PIS authorities signed a contract for a spyware system “over which they de facto had no control, because control remained in the hands of Israel and an Israeli company…whose cooperation with Israeli intelligence is, of course, beyond doubt”, said the prime minister.

“They paid money for a system that de facto transferred all possible data on Polish citizens, Polish opposition leaders and Polish independent prosecutors…to the Israeli side,” he added. “This is no longer [just] a scandal…We’re talking about a crime against the state.”

Two former heads of Polish security agencies have been charged over the use of Pegasus spyware under the former PiS government.

The pair, who deny wrongdoing, could be jailed for up to three years if found guilty of unlawfully allowing use of the spyware https://t.co/TWjQR74IYT

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 26, 2026

Later on Monday, a separate parliamentary committee set up by the ruling coalition to investigate the use of Pegasus also revealed unclassified sections of a report on its findings.

In addition to the information released by prosecutors, the commission also said that the CBA had never obtained the required IT security accreditation for Pegasus, meaning that it was used without meeting requirements for protecting classified information.

The commission’s chairwoman, Magdalena Sroka, also said that courts granting authorisation for the use of Pegasus were not informed of its full capabilities, such as the ability to access the entire contents of phones, reports broadcaster RMF.

💬 Jest to dokument o tym, jak władza publiczna w Polsce sięgnęła po narzędzie ingerujące w prawa obywatelskie – powiedziała przewodnicząca komisji śledczej ds. inwigilacji systemem Pegasus @MagdalenaSroka, prezentując raport z prac komisji.https://t.co/MzA9gj4M0Y

— PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) October 12, 2026

Legal proceedings are already underway against a number of former officials in relation to Pegasus. In February, prosecutors charged the former heads of the AWB and Military Counterintelligence Service (SKW) with abuse of power for approving the use of Pegasus despite being aware of legal shortcomings.

Previously, the former head of the CBA was charged with the same offence, while one of his deputies was charged with unlawfully disclosing material from surveillance of Roman Giertych, an MP from Tusk’s KO party who has also worked as a lawyer for Tusk and his family.

Last year, a former deputy justice minister from the PiS government, Michał Woś, was indicted to stand trial over his role in the alleged illegal use of justice ministry funds to help the CBA purchase Pegasus.

The United States wants Poland to join the G20 “as soon as possible” and intends to raise the issue with other members of the international forum at its forthcoming summit in December in Miami, the US State Department has told the Polish Press Agency (PAP).

Having previously endorsed Polish membership of the G20 in May, the US now says it intends to “continue discussions with G20 members this year on making Poland a full member as soon as possible”.

“Poland’s long-term and steady economic growth, combined with its growing leadership position in the international arena, make it an ideal participant,” the State Department told PAP.

Stany Zjednoczone oficjalnie zadeklarowały, że będą zabiegać o stałe członkostwo Polski w G20 https://t.co/lnZ583HIus

— Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) October 11, 2026

The G20, a major intergovernmental forum that brings together 19 major countries together with the European Union and the African Union, is set to meet at a golf resort owned by President Donald Trump in Miami on 14-15 December. Poland is also participating this year as a guest of the United States.

PAP reports that the US has proposed that one of the points in the final declaration adopted by leaders at the conclusion of the summit refer to Poland’s permanent membership. However, this would require the assent of all current members, including Russia.

The issue is likely to be discussed in a pre-summit online meeting of so-called “sherpas” negotiating the text of the declaration, reports PAP.

 

After visiting Washington earlier this month, Marcin Przydacz, the head of President Karol Nawrocki’s international policy office, said that joining the G20 permanently is “Plan A”, but acknowledged that receiving a consensus from existing member states made this variant difficult.

He added that Nawrocki would travel to London before the summit to discuss the possibility of continuing Poland’s guest status next year, when the UK will host the G20. At a meeting of G20 trade ministers last week, finance minister Andrzej Domański said that Poland has a good chance of being invited next year.

Nawrocki also plans to visit G20 members Saudi Arabia and Argentina to canvass for support for Poland’s membership bid, Przydacz has confirmed.

A third option would be for Poland to become a “permanent guest”, a status typically reserved for organisations like the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Group, but also held by Spain.

The case involves two Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian, all legal residents in Poland. The incident came to light in December 2025, after witnesses reported seeing the trio leading a goat through the centre of the city of Wałbrzych, before taking it to the back of a kebab bar.

After killing the animal, the men began butchering it for meat, which they were still portioning out when the police arrived. They told officers that the meat was intended for their own consumption. The kebab bar was closed for renovations at the time.

The men also said that such slaughter was customary in their home countries and they were unaware that, with limited exceptions, animals in Poland may generally be slaughtered only at authorised slaughterhouses, reports broadcaster RMF

 

A spokesman for prosecutors, Mariusz Pindera, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that the men’s unfamiliarity with Polish law did not “absolve them of the obligation to comply with the regulations”.

Prosecutors have therefore asked the court for a so-called conditional discontinuation of the case, a very common procedure under Polish law. Almost 25,000 such motions were submitted last year by prosecutors, citing the low social harm of the offences involved, reports Wirtualna Polska.

The court must now decide whether to accept or reject the prosecution’s motion. In the latter case, prosecutors would be required to proceed with an indictment against the suspects and seek a conviction. No hearing date on the motion has yet been set.

The sentence was handed down by the court of appeal in Lublin on Thursday, increasing by two years a jail term issued by a lower court earlier this year. The ruling is now final and binding.

The 51-year-old former Polish soldier, who has been named only as Paweł K. under privacy law, was detained by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) in April 2024.

Investigators found that the suspect had declared his willingness to collaborate with Russian intelligence and, between December 2022 and March 2024, had established contact via email and instant messaging with Russians involved in military operations against Ukraine, including army officers.

Prosecutors determined that Paweł K. had been assigned tasks including gathering and transmitting information regarding security at Rzeszów airport, which is the main hub for goods and people being transported in and out of Ukraine.

“These activities could have been used by Russian intelligence services, including in the context of planning a possible assassination attempt on the head of a foreign state, that is, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky,” wrote Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office earlier this year.

Last year, the head of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said that Paweł K. had been “recruited decades ago and firmly believed in the Soviet cause”. Polish prosecutors have not commented on that claim.

However, they did find that the suspect had declared his willingness to join Russian “sabotage structures”, including the Wagner mercenary group and Unit 29155 of the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence agency, which is tasked with carrying out destabilisation activities.

Paweł G. denied the accusations against him and claimed that he had actually been trying to help capture Russian war criminals by deceiving them into trusting him, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP).

His defence attorney argued that the information Paweł G. had transmitted regarding Rzeszów airport was “trivial and publicly available”, according to news website Onet.

 

In January this year, Paweł K. was found guilty of espionage and illegal possession of ammunition by the district court in the city of Zamość, which sentenced him to three and a half years in prison.

However, prosecutors appealed against that ruling, arguing that the suspect deserved a longer jail term of seven and a half years. In a judgement issued on Thursday, the Lublin appeals court agreed that Paweł G’s initial sentence had been “grossly lenient” and increased it by two years, reports PAP.

“Submitting an offer to work for…the intelligence service of a country that is at war with a country directly neighboring Poland, a country that is making quite extensive unfriendly gestures towards Poland, cannot be treated leniently,” said judge Artur Achrymowicz.

A sign installed to warn the public about damage caused by beavers has been destroyed by the beavers themselves, according to the Polish foresters who erected it.

The incident was reported in a post on social media by the forestry district of Lubliniec in southern Poland, which shared photos of the sign, which read “Warning! Damage caused by beavers”. The wooden post it was displayed on had been destroyed in an apparent beaver attack.

“We wanted to warn you about the potential consequences of beaver activity at the pond and the surrounding area – since beavers dig burrows under the road and fell trees near the pond – but the beavers didn’t want you to be warned, so…they cut down the oak post displaying the hazard notice,” wrote the foresters.

“So, if you are around the pond, please exercise caution; and if you spot a piece of wood sticking out of the ground that has been gnawed by beavers, just imagine there was a sign there reading ‘Warning! Damage caused by beavers’.”

Beavers were once almost hunted to extinction in Poland. By 1928, it was estimated that only 235 remained in the country. However, thanks to postwar efforts to reintroduce the animals into the Polish wilderness, the beaver population has grown and is currently estimated at around 150,000.

Ecologists note that beavers play an important role in tackling drought by retaining water through the dams they build. Those dams also create “oases of biodiversity”, notes the state water agency PGW WP.

However, the rodents can cause damage to roads, houses and farmland, which has led some to call for culls to keep beaver numbers down.

The brainchild of finance minister Andrzej Domański, the fund aims to foster the growth of Polish space technologies and bolster the country’s technological independence.

Poland’s space sector has expanded rapidly since the country joined the European Space Agency in 2012, moving from supplying components for foreign missions to developing its own satellites and space systems.

A key milestone came in 2024 with the launch of EagleEye, Poland’s largest satellite, which was designed and built by a consortium of Polish companies and research institutions. In 2025, a Pole went to space for the second time in history, 50 years after the first Polish astronaut’s flight.

The sector is now taking on larger international projects, while Russia’s war in Ukraine has highlighted the importance of domestic space capabilities for national security.

Wild Horse Nine | Dir Martin McDonagh | ★★★★☆

‘Two bumbling hitmen contemplate life and death on an ill-fated holiday’ could be the synopsis of Martin McDonagh’s near-perfect 2008 debut In Bruges, but in this instance it is in fact a synopsis of his new film Wild Horse Nine.

It’s fitting that his latest film is about people looking back at their loves and losses, because in many ways Wild Horse Nine feels like a mid-career retrospective of his own filmography. It touches upon many of the same themes he has explored in In Bruges and Seven Psychopaths and Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri and The Banshees of Inisherin, so aware of its predecessors that some of the funniest moments rely on at least a passing knowledge of his oeuvre. 

John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell replace Brendan Gleeson and Colin Farrell, each of them demonstrating large enough feet to fill those sizeable shoes. Opening in the American embassy in Chile in 1973, Wild Horse Nine is a kind of historical fiction, following two boorish CIA agents, Chris Carlisle (Malkovich) and Lee Chesterfield (Rockwell) as they embark on a mission to Easter Island. Carlisle hints to anyone who will listen that he was involved in some historic event; Chesterfield wishes he’d keep his mouth shut, at least when they’re in public. “We came down here to destabilise your government and it’s going great,” Carlisle quips to a pair of tourists at the airport.

Wild Horse Nine stars John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell

Malkovich, very much in his Elder Statesman era, is all prickly edges and prickly stubble, a man contemplating the end of things but still raging against the dying of the light, his bitterness a presence as imposing as the Easter Island heads they visit. Rockwell, meanwhile, appears unable to do much wrong these days, putting in a performance that’s both quietly charismatic and incredibly melancholy.

As in The Banshees of Inisherin, McDonagh is as interested in the landscape of this island as he is its visitors. Every second shot is a pan across a rugged cliffside or a silhouette of those famous heads. What is the point of it all, when we will one day be as anonymous as these nameless statues on an island of strangers?

This all sounds very bleak, and it is – but it’s also very funny. McDonagh’s trademark dry wit runs through this sad tale. There’s a wonderful skit about nations that make good cheeses being “gay” countries – France, England, Holland – while the straight countries – America and Russia – have no aptitude for cheese. 

McDonagh is a master at combining high and low culture, with jokes about dwarfs playing basketball nested beside a broad Shakespearean sweep about the terrible passage of time and the futility of Western imperialism. I’m not sure it hits quite the same highs as In Bruges or Banshees, but Wild Horse Nine is another sad, funny, moving film by a man who’s up there with Alexander Payne as a chronicler of the absurdity of the human condition.

AI’s impact on employment “is a slow-moving tsunami, but a tsunami nonetheless”, the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned, as the technology threatens to reshape six in ten jobs across advanced economies.

Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the IMF, said AI could affect 40 per cent of jobs worldwide, rising to 60 per cent in wealthier countries, with younger workers particularly vulnerable as employers automate entry-level tasks.

Speaking at the IMF’s annual meetings in Bangkok, Georgieva warned that the technology could eliminate some jobs, reduce the value of others and change the skills required across entire industries.

She said the impact was already becoming visible, with routine and repetitive jobs shrinking while demand for workers with AI skills increased.

An IMF study of the US labour market found that 10 per cent of jobs now require higher-level AI skills, which typically command better pay.

However, Georgieva warned that employment growth was increasingly concentrated in lower-paid sectors, including construction linked to data centre development and services.

“The net impact of the area we studied is actually positive. But that’s not a story to celebrate because it is positive on the side of lower-paying jobs”, she said.

The IMF chief singled out younger workers as particularly exposed, warning that the disappearance of routine jobs could remove traditional routes into professional careers.

“Normally, they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then grow up the ranks”, she said.

London workers face greatest AI exposure

The warning carries particular significance for Britain, where London has been identified as one of the world’s most AI-exposed labour markets.

An OECD report published in July found that nearly four in five jobs in the capital were highly exposed to generative AI, reflecting London’s concentration of professional and administrative roles.

Ian Hargreaves, partner at Quillon Law, highlighted that many believe whistleblowing should be a “public and social duty” rather than a profit-making exercise.

He added: “Whistleblowers must also be protected against retaliation or more sinister treatment, which is covered to an extent under employment legislation, although arguably not as effectively as it should be.”

He said: “It is worth remembering why the SFO has been calling for the introduction of a whistleblower reward scheme. It is for intelligence, not evidence.”

Lucy Blake, partner at Jenner & Block, pointed out a massive hurdle if whistleblowers do take the stand. Unlike the US, where most cases end in plea deals, the UK has many contested jury trials. “It will be interesting to see how juries respond to that evidence, and whether it adds weight to the case for judge-only trials in complex fraud cases, a proposal that remains in the Courts and Tribunals Bill as it returns to Parliament,” she added.

Risks to business culture

Mackie, an employment lawyer, explained it will directly “undermine internal corporate governance.”

“It is never helpful to have to question the motives of someone reporting an alleged crime, which will always be a risk, and so paying people to do so is fundamentally flawed,” she added.

“It is however important to ensure that any scheme introduced in the UK complements, rather than replaces, proactive fraud prevention measures,” she added.

Britain must compete to keep its wealthy as countries like Oman offer greater stability, lower taxes and less crime, says Damien Phillips

In her speech to close the Conservative conference, Kemi Badenoch’s claim that Britain’s “super wealthy… have all gone” might have been a rhetorical flourish but the exodus of our millionaires is real and is only going to get worse 

Britain suffered a tenfold increase in high-net worth individuals fleeing high-tax Britain in just three years, losing around 1,600 millionaires in 2022 and an estimated 16,500 in 2025. Earlier this week, property tycoon David Reuben who shares a family fortune of £28bn, confirmed he had quit the UK for Monaco. In September, we lost hedge-fund billionaire Chris Rokos to Greece. Barely a month seems to go by without another prominent millionaire deciding that Britain is hostile territory for them. 

Recent analysis of the Bloomberg Billionaire’s Index, which didn’t even include Reuben’s departure, showed that ultra-wealthy people worth roughly £121bn have left Britain since Labour came to power in 2024 – this represents more than half of the billionaire wealth associated with the UK.

Competing jurisdications

Many countries like Italy, Switzerland and Monaco are luring them away with a simple proposition – come here and you can preserve your wealth. Switzerland is selling certainty and capital preservation, while Italy allows new residents to avoid being taxed normally and instead pay a €300,000 annual lump sum on foreign income for up to 15 years. 

Others, like the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Singapore and the United States combine favourable treatment of wealth with enormous opportunities to deploy it. For founders and investors, the US offers vast pools of venture capital, highly liquid property markets, tech clusters and enormous consumer demand. Many of those leaving Britain want to create new wealth, not just protect what they have, hence why the US poached 7,500 UK millionaires in 2025 alone. 

Research suggests that global competition for millionaires is also as much about security as it is about tax and opportunities for growth. Wealthy families are looking for places where they and their children feel physically safe and where the political and legal environment is predictable. With nearly nine in ten Brits believing crime and anti-social behaviour are a major national problem and 67 per cent feeling that crime has become worse in the past year, Britain is increasingly unattractive to anyone who doesn’t have to stay here.  

To our chagrin, governments are now actively sharpening their bids to the mobile wealthy and combining all three of these elements into a single deal. Henley’s Wealth Report 2026 singled out Qatar, Bahrain and Oman as “broadening their offerings” as competition for international capital and talent intensifies. 

Oman for instance, whose Sultan is headed to Britain later this month for a state visit, launched a renewable 10-year Golden Residency programme last year aimed at business owners, entrepreneurs and investors that allows them to bring their families and creates a stable, long-term base from which to own, invest in, and run businesses in the country. 

With no income tax and very efficient development, in the World Competitiveness Rankings in 2026 Oman rose to 25th in the world out of 70 economies – just one place behind the UK. On top of this, it ranks third in the world for perceived safety, with 94 per cent of residents saying they feel safe walking alone at night.   

This is the kind of multifaceted package that Britain is now competing against. Yet instead of upping our game, we are talking about yet another tax raising Budget, while Labour-aligned voices call for a wealth tax. The millionaire flight will simply intensify because, as Michael Corleone puts it in The Godfather Part II, Britain’s offer is this: “Nothing”.

Damien Phillips is a fellow of The Cobden Centre and a regular contributor to The Spectator. He has written for CapX, The Critic, ConservativeHome and The Telegraph

Some 42 bids for London-listed firms are currently ongoing with a total market capitalisation of £74bn, according to a new note from Peel Hunt. The figure is more than double the £35bn from the entirety of 2025 across 40 bids.

Overseas bidders make up 64 per cent of the 2026 figures, broadly flat with the previous year.

But the buoyant deals market has come amid a “dearth of IPOs”. Since the start of 2023 there have been 166 bids for firms with a price tag over £100m with the collective value topping £180bn. This is compared to just 11 IPOs above £100 for a total value of £6bn.

“To say that the UK has a problem retaining its companies and listing new ones would be a massive understatement,” said Charles Hall, head of research at Peel Hunt. 

He added the number and value of bids for UK firms were running at “exceptionally high levels, raising concerns that the UK equity market is seeing a material depopulation”.

Airtel Money completed its IPO on the London market last week with a valuation of £5.3bn, marking the biggest listing in five years. It marked the first time since 2021 that the London Stock Exchange landed an IPO north of £1bn.

The City has struggled to compete with the lure of US markets and lost some of its top talent to exchanges across the Atlantic. Money transfer firm Wise downgraded its London listing in favour of New York last year in a major hit to the City bourse.

Since 2023, seven UK giants have shifted their listings, blowing a £120bn hole in the London market. In the same period, seven UK-based firms have also opted to IPO overseas.

“The pace of delistings vs listings in the UK is widening,” one banker told City AM, adding the European markets were “massively lagging the US”.

Calls for government intervention

London AI infrastructure firm Nscale filed for a US listing targeting a $35bn valuation earlier this year, pouring cold water on hopes from stock exchange officials and ministers of attracting high-growth tech talent.

Hall suggested a series of intervention measures to boost equity markets, including shaking up the capital gains regime for domestic and overseas investors and fast-tracking index inclusion. 

“The good news is that turbocharging UK equity markets is not difficult and can be done at pace,” he said.

City minister Lucy Rigby told City AM that capital markets reform was “not a job done” and the government was “continually looking for ways that we can ensure we’re being as competitive as possible”.

Hall pointed to ditching stamp duty on shares as a key lever to “remove friction and enhance UK competitiveness,” adding it makes “no sense for a UK investor to have a higher transaction cost for buying shares in a UK company than a US business”.
