]]> Wiremind, a Paris-based AI software company serving the transport, air cargo, and events industries, has closed a €35 million funding round, its first since being founded over a decade ago.

The round brings three new investors: IronWave (formerly Wendel Growth), Bpifrance Investissement through its Large Venture fund, and Seaya Andromeda. The company said Wiremind’s co-founders, CEO Colin Girault-Matz and CTO Charles Pierre, will remain majority shareholders and retain control of the business.

“In twelve years, and without a single euro of outside capital, Colin, Charles and their teams have built systems that today drive the revenue of the largest rail and air operators,” said Victoire Laurenty, founder and General Partner of IronWave (formerly Wendel Growth).

Founded in October 2014, Wiremind is a bootstrapped company driven by its founders’ passion for data visualisation, tech and optimisation. They first crossed paths at SNCF, where they identified a gap in the market for machine learning-powered tools to help transport operators manage revenue and capacity more effectively.

Its flagship product is called CAYZN, an AI-first revenue management system for passenger transport operators. After being adopted by leading transportation companies, the system has reportedly delivered revenue gains between 5 and 15% on average. In 2025, CAYZN’s annual recurring revenue grew 81% year over year. The company has expanded its portfolio to include PAXONE, a next-generation inventory and distribution platform, CARGOSTACK for air cargo management, and EVENTORI, an AI-driven ticketing and revenue management platform for sports clubs and event organisers.

The fundraiser marks a significant milestone for a company that has operated entirely without outside capital while remaining profitable. In 2025, the company said its revenue grew 67% across the board, and it now works with more than 80 clients, 23 of which joined over the year.

“Charles and I began our careers more than fifteen years ago in the rail and aviation industries, so we have a unique understanding of the challenges our clients face. It is this first-hand knowledge that we leveraged to grow Wiremind over the years, while staying completely self-financed and investing in our own R&D,” said Girault-Matz, co-founder and CEO, Wiremind.

He added, “Today, we’re accelerating our efforts given the speed at which the market is adopting artificial intelligence tools. This financing round will allow us to reach rapidly growing geographic markets where decisions on technology investments are being made right now.”

The funding will be used to support two strategic priorities: expanding into new international markets and deepening investment in AI research and development. The company will continue its growth in South America and extend its reach into the Middle East and APAC regions, building upon its success in Europe and North America.

]]> Monte Carlo Capital (MCC), the Monaco-based early-stage venture firm investing at Seed in DeepTech and tech-enabled innovators, today announced a €13 million ($15 million) first close of Fund II, with a target of €26 million ($30 million).

This comes after the close of Fund I at over €11 million in 2025 – as reported by EU-Startups. Most Fund I LPs have recommitted, and Fund II has already made five investments.

“Reaching a $15 million first close on Fund II is a strong vote of confidence from our investors, and we have already put that capital to work in five companies. Our approach hasn’t changed: get onto outstanding cap tables early, invest alongside the world’s leading VCs, and keep backing our best companies as they scale through our SPVs. We only invest where we see a credible path to a multi-billion-dollar outcome,” says Ian Sosso, founder and Managing Partner, Monte Carlo Capital.

Monte Carlo Capital’s Fund II first close comes amid continued fundraising activity among European venture capital firms targeting DeepTech, AI and other emerging technologies in 2026.

Recent EU-Startups coverage includes Munich-based Vanagon Ventures’ €20 million fund for pre-Seed DeepTech and AI startups, London-based Project Ventures’ €5.8 million vehicle targeting university-linked ventures, and Ruya Ventures’ €43 million DeepTech fund.

Larger vehicles include Paris-based 360 Capital’s €85 million Poli360 2 fund, Berlin-based Merantix Capital’s €103 million AI fund, London-based Transition Ventures’ €128 million Fund II and French VC Elaia’s €134 million DeepTech Seed fund.

Together, these announcements represent approximately €519 million in disclosed fund capital, rising to €532 million when including MCC’s latest first close.

Founded in 2009 by Ian Sosso, MCC combines a lean fund with co-investment SPVs. Before launching MCC’s funds, Ian built a track record as an angel investor, leading over 50 syndicates and acting as lead investor up to Series B.

He is a board member of the European Business Angels Network (EBAN), which named him Best European Early-Stage Investor in 2019.

Today’s announcement comes 3 years after MCC’s launch of its first fund in 2023. Fund II invests primarily at Seed, and selectively at pre-Seed and Series A, with a focus on sectors such as DeepTech, AI, SpaceTech, and enterprise software.

Current portfolio companies include:

  • StarCloud – Fastest YC company ever to reach unicorn status. Now valued at €2 billion ($2.3 billion).
  • Scout AI – Reportedly, the largest DefenceTech Series A in US history, at €357 million ($400 million).

The post Starfunding: 10 of Europe’s biggest celebrity-backed startup deals appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Celebrity investment in startups is nothing new, but the range of businesses attracting famous backers is expanding. Beyond traditional endorsements and brand partnerships, celebrities are putting capital into companies working on artificial intelligence, digital healthcare, clean energy, biotechnology and other emerging sectors.

Some are investing directly, while others participate through venture capital firms or dedicated investment vehicles. Their involvement can bring not only funding but also international visibility, industry connections and strategic expertise.

With that in mind, we’ve put together 10 notable celebrity-backed startup deals across Europe. The figures below reflect publicly reported investment amounts, funding rounds or financing arrangements, depending on what has been disclosed. Individual contributions are identified wherever possible.

Kylian Mbappé – Alan (France): €100 million funding round

French football superstar Kylian Mbappé, a World Cup winner and Real Madrid forward, became an investor and ambassador for Paris-based health-tech company Alan in March 2026 through his investment vehicle, Coalition Capital.

Founded in 2016, Alan provides digital health insurance and healthcare services. Earlier that month, the company secured a €100 million funding round, bringing its valuation to approximately €5 billion. It subsequently raised another €480 million in June 2026.

Although Mbappé’s individual investment was not disclosed, he is collaborating with Alan on initiatives related to preventive healthcare, mental health, nutrition and physical activity.

Leonardo DiCaprio – SolarMente (Spain): €50 million financing agreement

American actor and environmental advocate Leonardo DiCaprio, known for films including Titanic, Inception and The Revenant, became an investor in Barcelona-based ClimateTech startup SolarMente in 2024.

Unfortunately for both the founders and Di Caprio’s invesmtent, the company went bankrupt in April of 2026. SolarMente helped households access solar energy through a subscription model that reduces the need for large upfront installation costs.

That has not stopped Leo however, as he has continued his investment trends since then, having this week invested an undisclosed amount in Stockholm-based Energy-as-a-Service company Elvy.

Emma Watson – FabricNano (United Kingdom): €10.5 million Series A

British actress and activist Emma Watson, internationally recognised for playing Hermione Granger in the Harry Potter film series, joined the investors in London-based BioTech startup FabricNano in 2021.

Founded in 2018, FabricNano develops cell-free biomanufacturing technology designed to make industrial production processes more efficient and reduce dependence on fossil fuel-derived materials. Its technology uses immobilised enzymes to support the production of chemicals and other materials.

Pau Gasol – Luzia (Spain): €9.5 million funding round

Spanish basketball legend Pau Gasol, a two-time NBA champion with the Los Angeles Lakers and one of Europe’s most successful basketball players, backed Madrid-based artificial intelligence startup Luzia through his investment vehicle, Gasol16 Ventures.

Luzia develops a generative AI assistant accessible through messaging platforms such as WhatsApp and Telegram, allowing users to interact with artificial intelligence without downloading a separate application.

Elton John – Audoo (United Kingdom): €4.75 million funding round

British singer-songwriter Sir Elton John, whose career spans more than five decades and includes hits such as Rocket Man and Your Song, became an investor in London-based music technology startup Audoo in 2023.

Founded in 2018, Audoo develops audio recognition technology that identifies music played in public places such as shops, restaurants and gyms. Its goal is to provide more accurate data to music rights organisations and help artists receive fairer royalty payments.

Ibai Llanos – Plesh (Spain): €3.75 million funding round

Spanish streamer and entrepreneur Ibai Llanos, known for his massive online audience, the boxing event La Velada del Año and his involvement in the Kings League, entered the FoodTech sector in October 2026.

Together with former Barcelona footballer Gerard Piqué, Llanos led a €3.75 million financing round in Barcelona-based startup Plesh, a company developing chocolate snacks without added sugar.

Snoop Dogg – Sanity Group (Germany): €3 million investment

American rapper and entrepreneur Snoop Dogg, a prominent figure in hip-hop since the 1990s, has developed a broad business portfolio that includes technology and cannabis-related ventures.

Through Casa Verde Capital, the venture capital firm he co-founded, Snoop Dogg is connected an investment in Berlin-based Sanity Group in November 2021.

Founded in 2018, Sanity Group develops products and businesses in medical cannabis and consumer health, combining pharmaceutical expertise with regulated healthcare distribution.

Novak Djokovic – waterdrop (Austria): Seven-figure investment

Serbian tennis champion Novak Djokovic, one of the most successful players in the history of the sport.

In 2023, he became an investor and brand ambassador for Vienna-based startup waterdrop. Founded in 2016, waterdrop develops compact hydration cubes that dissolve in water.

Djokovic made a significant seven-figure investment, according to reports from January 2023. Although the exact figure was not disclosed, his personal commitment represents one of the clearer examples of an individually attributed celebrity investment in a European startup.

Diogo Dalot – Bioniq (United Kingdom): Over €1 million investment

Portuguese professional footballer Diogo Dalot, who plays for Manchester United and the Portuguese national team, joined London-based HealthTech startup Bioniq as an investor in March 2025.

Founded in 2019, Bioniq creates personalised nutritional supplements using blood biomarker data and AI-driven analysis to develop formulations tailored to individual needs.

Dalot contributed over €1 million to the company, joining fellow Portuguese footballer Cristiano Ronaldo, who had invested in Bioniq the previous year.

David Beckham – Guild Esports (United Kingdom): €272k investment

English football icon David Beckham, a former Manchester United and Real Madrid player and one of the world’s most commercially recognisable athletes, entered competitive gaming by investing in London-based Guild Esports in 2020.

Founded in 2019, Guild Esports was established to build professional gaming teams, develop esports talent and compete in international tournaments across major video game titles.

In June 2020, Beckham invested through his business DB Ventures, acquiring shares in the company ahead of its listing on the London Stock Exchange later that year.

Summary

From digital health and AI to biotechnology, solar power and esports, these investments demonstrate how celebrities are becoming participants in Europe’s entrepreneurial ecosystem.

While the amounts and structures vary considerably, the involvement of globally recognised figures can give young companies access to networks, visibility and opportunities that extend beyond traditional startup financing. At the same time, the deals highlight an important distinction: a celebrity’s participation in a multimillion-euro funding round does not necessarily mean that the celebrity invested the full amount personally.

As more athletes, entertainers and creators establish investment vehicles of their own, celebrity-backed startups are likely to remain a visible part of Europe’s innovation landscape.

]]> SpectaCell, a new Ghent-based startup specialising in next-generation cell therapy analytics, has announced its official launch with €6 million in Seed funding. The company has spun out of imec, VIB and Ghent University. 

The round was led by imec.xpand, with participation from PMV’s Flanders Future Tech Fund, InnovationQuarter Capital, Qbic and VIB. 

Tony Montoye, CEO and co-founder of SpectaCell, said, “Breakthrough medicines need breakthrough tools. Researchers need to know much earlier which candidates deserve further investment and why. We are building a new standard in cell analysis: detailed insight, results within hours and a simple workflow that connects research with manufacturing.

“Together with our biopharma partners, we will turn that vision into a platform for developing better treatments more efficiently. And ultimately, that is what we want to make possible for patients: better medicines, sooner.”

Founded in 2026 by Mathieu Rabaey, Veronique De Vroey, Jan Van de Velde, and Tony Montoye, SpectaCell is a Belgian life sciences company developing a next-generation cell analysis platform for drug development and manufacturing. 

Its proprietary technology combines digital imaging and data analysis to measure how treatments affect individual cells.

According to the company, immunotherapies are opening new ways to treat cancer and diseases of the immune system. Yet predicting which candidates will work in patients and producing them consistently remain major challenges. It notes that developers need a clearer view of what a treatment actually does, earlier in the process. Slow, fragmented testing can leave critical gaps in that understanding and delay decisions while patients wait.

SpectaCell claims to tackle these testing bottlenecks with a next-generation cell analysis platform that measures how treatments affect individual cells. Applications include cell therapies and T-cell engagers that help immune cells recognise and attack cancer cells. 

“Developers of new immune therapies need to understand what happens when a treatment meets its target: does it kill a cancer cell, for example, and how do individual cells respond? Many existing tests provide only part of that picture because they measure indirect signals or averages across a sample. Important differences between cells can disappear in those averages,” the company mentioned in the press release. 

SpectaCell highlighted that it combines chip-based imaging with data analysis to track large numbers of individual cells and their interactions directly, at high resolution and over time. The technology does not require fluorescent labels that can interfere with cell behaviour. The company is developing an easy-to-use, cartridge-based instrument designed to deliver these insights in hours rather than days.

It is targeting pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies and specialist manufacturers worldwide. The company is developing a single platform for use from early research and process development through to routine manufacturing quality checks. The Belgian company says it will enable researchers to compare drug candidates, development teams to improve production processes, and manufacturers to assess whether each batch meets required performance standards.

Benoit Devogelaere, Partner at imec.xpand, said, “SpectaCell brings together disruptive semiconductor technology, an experienced team and a major commercial opportunity in drug development and manufacturing. 

“We are convinced that SpectaCell can become essential to how new medicines are selected, developed and produced. With applications across cell therapies, T-cell engagers and other advanced treatments, we see the potential to set a new industry standard and build a globally competitive life-sciences business. We are proud to lead this round and back that ambition.”

The company plans to use this capital to fund further development and commercialisation of the platform with pharmaceutical and biotechnology partners.

]]> Sava Technologies, a London-based HealthTech company developing a wearable biosensor platform that detects molecules just beneath the skin, today announced a €32.08 million ($36 million) Series B round to fund manufacturing scale-up and commercial readiness.

The round was led by Ascensia, with participation from institutional investors Balderton Capital, Norrsken VC, Simplyhealth Ventures, JamJar Investments, Pentland Ventures and others. In July 2025, the company announced a €16.6 million Series A funding round led by Balderton Capital and Pentland Ventures.  

This funding brings the company’s total funding to €60.6 million ($68 million). The UK startup also announced an agreement appointing Ascensia, a subsidiary of PHC Holdings Corporation (TYO 6523), as its commercialisation and distribution partner, initially in Europe.

Renato Circi, co-founder and Co-CEO of Sava, said, “For decades, continuous monitoring has been held back by the same legacy technology. This is about to change. We’re thrilled to be partnering with Ascensia, a global powerhouse in the space, to deliver, as a first step, something radically better to millions of people with diabetes.”

Founded in 2019 by Imperial College London bioengineers Renato Circi and Rafaël Michali, Sava is a venture-backed consumer and medical device company behind a next-generation glucose microsensor. After five years in stealth, it emerged in June 2024 and announced that it had raised more than €7.4 million in a Seed funding round led by Balderton Capital and Exor Ventures. 

The company says it has developed a wearable built on its proprietary microsensor technology that measures molecules just beneath the skin, painlessly and continuously. While the platform starts with glucose, it is also designed to track other biomarkers, opening the door to continuous sensing far beyond diabetes. 

According to Sava, its microsensors are about ten times shorter than the filament in traditional continuous glucose monitors (CGMs), reducing disruption to the skin while still reaching interstitial fluid. 

The company notes that since the technology was designed from the outset for high-volume manufacture, it is built to reach people at scale. It is now focusing on commercialisation and has therefore partnered with Ascensia to get there at scale. 

Basel-based Ascensia is a member of PHC Group and was established in 2016 through the acquisition of Bayer Diabetes Care by PHC Holdings Corporation. Ascensia sells its products in more than 90 countries, with direct commercial organisations in 29 markets. Its portfolio includes the CONTOUR range of blood glucose monitoring systems.

Peter Bodlund, Chief Executive Officer of Ascensia, commented, “Microsensor technology has the potential to transform the day-to-day monitoring experience for people with diabetes. By bringing together Sava’s innovative technology with Ascensia’s deep diabetes expertise, strong reputation and commercial capabilities, we have an exciting opportunity to address important unmet needs in diabetes care. This is an exciting step for Ascensia as we continue to broaden our portfolio and pursue our ambition to simplify and improve life for people with diabetes.”

Sava is also planning a pivotal clinical study this year and is targeting CE approval for non-adjunctive use. This means the device could be used to make insulin dosing decisions without routine fingerstick confirmation—the standard required for a CGM to replace, rather than supplement, blood glucose testing. Subject to CE approval, Ascensia will lead the commercial launch, starting in Europe.

The company plans to use this capital to fund manufacturing scale-up and commercial readiness.

The post EXCLUSIVE: Ecosia founder clarifies move away from Mistral – It’s about open models, not China appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Ecosia’s decision to drop French AI provider Mistral is not a move towards Chinese technology, but rather a shift towards more affordable, energy-efficient open AI models, founder and CEO Christian Kroll clarified in a conversation with EU-Startups.

“We’ll probably be using Melious.ai in future. Unlike Mistral, this is a European company that offers high-quality, affordable AI inference powered by green electricity,” shared Christian in an exclusive interview.

The Berlin-based search engine recently made headlines after POLITICO reported that it was replacing Mistral with open models, including Chinese offerings such as Alibaba’s Qwen, Z.ai’s GLM and Moonshot AI’s Kimi.

However, Christian stressed that the company’s focus is on open models rather than their country of origin. These offer lower costs, greater flexibility and reduced energy consumption, aligning with Ecosia’s environmental mission.

Addressing concerns about political censorship in Chinese AI models, Christian explained that Ecosia can switch to alternative models when dealing with sensitive subjects, such as questions about Taiwan. The company is also working to eliminate political biases from its AI-generated answers.

The models are accessed through German platform Melious, which operates on European infrastructure powered by low-carbon energy. This allows Ecosia to use internationally developed AI while keeping its infrastructure and data processing in Europe.

“Europe needs its own AI capabilities. At Melious, we run open-weight models on European infrastructure powered by clean energy, outside the reach of the US CLOUD Act. Whether a model was built in Europe, the US or China, it’s simply a set of weights on our servers. It can’t send data back to its makers, and customer data is never retained or used for training. We’re proud to work with Ecosia to show that sovereign AI can deliver strong performance at a fair price,” CEO and co-founder Simon Jakobs told EU-Startups.

Christian also reiterated his concerns about Mistral’s European sovereignty, arguing that its reliance on foreign investors, particularly from the United States, undermines its independence.

This follows a period of significant expansion for Paris-based Mistral AI. In September 2026, the company secured €3 billion in Series D funding, led by Samsung Electronics, at a valuation exceeding €21 billion. The investment followed €722 million in debt financing announced in March to develop its first large-scale data centre near Paris, as well as a €1.7 billion Series C led by Dutch semiconductor equipment manufacturer ASML in September 2025.

Its latest funding round included US investors such as Andreessen Horowitz, Nvidia and Salesforce Ventures, alongside European backers including ASML and Bpifrance. Mistral also participated in a €2.9 million investment in Italian infrastructure startup Clastix.

These come amid wider investment in European AI infrastructure, with financing announcements covered by EU-Startups in 2026 totalling approximately €6.2 billion, including Mistral’s own funding.

Christian contrasted this with Ecosia’s own funding history. The company grew largely without external financing, receiving early backing from German entrepreneur Tim Schumacher. In 2018, Ecosia adopted a steward-ownership structure that prevents the company from being sold or distributing profits to shareholders.

For Ecosia, the switch reflects a broader vision for European technology: rather than depending on individual AI developers, European companies can build competitive, independent services using open models running on European infrastructure.

For Mistral, however, this development implies a loss of trust in what is considered one of Europe’s most promising AI companies.

]]> Klarent (formerly fore ai), a Zurich-based autonomous software testing startup, has closed a €7.13 million Seed funding round.

The round was led by London-based Mosaic Ventures, with participation from Moonfire Ventures and a number of prominent angel investors, including Jürgen Galler, a former Director at Google, Harris Barton, and AngelInvest Ventures, among others.

“With AI, code generation is scaling faster than our ability to test it, so QA will become the key bottleneck. Asheem and Momo saw this at Google before most of the industry did. What convinced us was their insistence on determinism – using AI to write tests, not to run them – which is why enterprises are trusting Klarent in production. We’re delighted to back the team as they expand to the US,” said Chandar Lal, Partner, Mosaic Ventures.

The startup was founded in 2023 by two ex-Google engineers, Asheem Panakkat, who serves as CEO, and Momchil Ivanov, who serves as CTO. Panikkar spent more than a decade at Google leading teams on Shopping and Lens, while Ivanov worked as a Staff Software Engineer focused on information retrieval. Together, they spotted how the explosion in code being written as large language models became more capable meant the systems used to verify that code were nowhere near ready to keep up.

Their solution: deterministic autonomy. Instead of leaning on large language models to run tests directly, Klarent’s agents use LLMs only to author test code. Once written, the test code executes in a deterministic, repeatable manner, combining the adaptability of AI with the rigour expected in production engineering. There is also a human-in-the-loop verification layer on top, ensuring customers pay only for verified outcomes. 

“At Google, Momo and I could see two things coming at once: LLMs were getting better fast, and the amount of software being created was about to explode. The question that wouldn’t leave us was the feedback loop. How do you keep these coding agents honest? We began by building evals for LLMs and quickly realised the bigger opportunity was QA itself. As AI writes more of the world’s code, testing stops being a cost centre and becomes the thing that determines whether any of that code can be trusted,” said Panakkat.

Their approach has already won over enterprise clients across Europe. JD Sports, Swiss media group NZZ, and mobility company Sixt all use the platform. At JD Sports, Klarent’s AI agents automate multi-system workflows across the e-commerce pipeline, an automation that the retailer said its own teams could not replicate.

The funding will be used by Klarent to support its entry into the United States, building on the momentum seen with its European enterprise customers. The company also plans to grow its engineering team and broaden its cross-platform testing capabilities across web and mobile. It is also pushing into financial services, working with banks and insurance firms where the cost of a broken software release can be catastrophically high.

 .et_pb_row_inner { width: 100%; }
 .et_pb_column { position: relative; } </style> <style id="sie-custom-header-inline">/* ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
 SIE Custom Header — v1.1.2
 Zero-CLS, no JavaScript layout shifts.
 No panoramic image — lean 64px nav bar only.
 backdrop-filter is intentionally NOT used on .sie-hdr__bar.
 Any element with backdrop-filter becomes a CSS containing block for
 position:fixed descendants, which would trap the user-ui mobile bottom bar
 (position:fixed; bottom:0) inside the header instead of the viewport.
 ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ */
/* ── Root variables ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
:root {
 --sie-hdr-brand:       #0056b3;        /* SIE brand blue                      */
 --sie-hdr-brand-light: #1a6fc4;
 --sie-hdr-bar-h:       64px;           /* nav bar height — fixed, prevents CLS */
 --sie-hdr-bar-bg:      #0056b3;        /* solid — no backdrop-filter needed   */
 --sie-hdr-bar-border:  rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.15);
}
/* ── Wrapper ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr {
 width: 100%;
 display: block;
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 /* Own stacking context so dropdowns render above Divi page content */
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1000;
}
/* ── Navigation bar ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__bar {
 height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter here — it would trap position:fixed children
 (user-ui mobile bottom bar) inside this element instead of viewport */
 border-bottom: 1px solid var(--sie-hdr-bar-border);
}
.sie-hdr__inner {
 max-width: 1280px;
 height: 100%;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 32px;
}
/* ── Logo ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__logo {
 flex-shrink: 0;
 text-decoration: none;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-img {
 height: 54px;
 width: auto;
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-text {
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 17px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #fff;
 letter-spacing: -0.01em;
 white-space: nowrap;
}
/* ── Desktop navigation ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__nav {
 flex: 1;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list {
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list li {
 position: relative;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 padding: 8px 14px;
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 text-decoration: none;
 border-radius: 8px;
 transition: background 0.15s ease, color 0.15s ease;
 white-space: nowrap;
 min-height: 48px; /* WCAG touch target */
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a:hover,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle:hover,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 color: #fff;
}
/* ── Resources dropdown ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: none;
 position: absolute;
 top: calc(100% + 6px);
 left: 0;
 min-width: 240px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 12px;
 box-shadow: 0 12px 40px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.18);
 padding: 8px 0;
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 z-index: 9999;
}
/* CSS-only hover on desktop */
@media (hover: hover) {
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown,
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:focus-within > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
 }
}
/* JS-toggled state (mobile / keyboard) */
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown li {
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 display: block;
 padding: 10px 18px;
 font-size: 13.5px;
 color: #003B73;
 font-weight: 500;
 border-radius: 0;
 min-height: unset;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: #f0f7ff;
 color: #0b5394;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transition: transform 0.2s ease;
}
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transform: rotate(180deg);
}
/* ── Mobile hamburger ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: none;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: center;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 5px;
 width: 44px;
 height: 44px;
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 0;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger span {
 display: block;
 width: 22px;
 height: 2px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 2px;
 transition: transform 0.25s ease, opacity 0.25s ease;
}
/* Animate to ✕ when open */
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(1) {
 transform: translateY(7px) rotate(45deg);
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(2) {
 opacity: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(3) {
 transform: translateY(-7px) rotate(-45deg);
}
/* ── User-UI icon bar integration ────────────────────────────────────────────
 user-ui.php's desktop bar uses position:absolute; top:20px; right:30px — that
 was designed for Divi's header context. Inside our flex .sie-hdr__inner we
 need it as a normal flex child instead.
 Fixed-position children (auth drawer, mobile bar, destinations panel) are
 unaffected — position:fixed is always viewport-relative provided no ancestor
 has backdrop-filter, transform, or perspective (we intentionally avoid all
 three on .sie-hdr__bar).
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 position: static !important;
 top: auto !important;
 right: auto !important;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
/* Align our mobile breakpoint (860px) with user-ui's desktop/mobile split */
@media (min-width: 861px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {

 }
}
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: none !important;
 }
}
/* Leonardo icon in the nav bar.
 user-ui's default .se-ai-icon is 86×86 px (fine for the mobile bottom bar),
 but that overflows our 64px-tall nav bar. Override to a crisp 36px square —
 the webp source is already high-res so it stays sharp at 2× on retina. */
.sie-hdr .se-ai-icon {
 width:  36px !important;
 height: 36px !important;
 border-radius: 50%;
 object-fit: cover;
}
/* Icon colours inside the header.
 user-ui defaults: map icon is #2f6fed (dark blue) and heart is #F44336 (red).
 The map icon is nearly invisible on our #0056b3 bar — lift all icons to white.
 The heart keeps its red via the !important below so favourited items still pop. */
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.85) !important;
}
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon:hover {
 color: #fff !important;
}
/* Fav heart — keep the red so it reads as "save" */
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link {
 color: #ff6b6b !important;   /* slightly lighter red, readable on blue */
}
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link:hover {
 color: #ff4444 !important;
}
/* ── Responsive ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 :root {
 --sie-hdr-bar-h: 56px;
 }
 .sie-hdr {
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 }
 .sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: flex;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav {

 position: absolute;
 top: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);           /* flush below the nav bar */
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter — same reason as .sie-hdr__bar */
 padding: 12px 0 20px;
 clip-path: inset(0 0 100% 0);       /* collapses upward — no CLS */
 transition: clip-path 0.3s ease;
 z-index: 9998;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav.is-open {
 clip-path: inset(0);
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list {
 flex-direction: column;
 align-items: flex-start;
 gap: 0;
 padding: 0 16px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list a,
 .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 width: 100%;
 font-size: 15px;
 padding: 12px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 position: static;
 box-shadow: none;
 border-radius: 0;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.06);
 padding: 4px 0 4px 16px;
 margin: 4px 0;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.8);
 font-size: 14px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.08);
 color: #fff;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 480px) {
 .sie-hdr__inner {
 padding: 0 16px;
 gap: 16px;
 }
}

.sie-hdr__dropdown::before {
 content: "";
 position: absolute;
 top: -10px;
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 height: 10px;
}

.sie-dest-panel,
#sie-auth-drawer,
#sie-lead-form-drawer,
.sie-finder-overlay {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;

.sie-field-hero{position: relative; 
 left: 50%;
 right: 50%;
 margin-left: -50vw;
 margin-right: -50vw;
 width: 100vw; 
 min-height: 480px;
 max-height: 560px;
 background-size: cover;
 background-position: center 40%;
 background-repeat: no-repeat; 
 background-color: #003B73;
 overflow: hidden;
 margin-bottom: 0;}
.sie-field-hero--no-image{background: linear-gradient(
 135deg,
 var(--field-color, #003B73) 0%,
 color-mix(in srgb, var(--field-color, #003B73) 65%, #000) 100%
 );}
.sie-field-hero__bg-img{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center 40%;
 z-index: 0;
 display: block;}
.sie-field-hero__overlay{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 1;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.90) 0%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.60) 38%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.25) 65%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.12) 100%
 );
 display: flex;
 align-items: flex-end;
 padding-bottom: 52px;}
.sie-field-hero__inner{width: 100%;
 max-width: 1100px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 32px;}
.sie-field-hero__label{display: block;
 font-size: 13px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.75);
 margin-bottom: 12px;
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-hero__label a{color: inherit;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__label a:hover{color: #fff;
 text-decoration: underline;}
.sie-field-category-badge{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 7px;
 padding: 6px 14px;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.18);
 border: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.35);
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 12px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 20px;
 margin-bottom: 14px;
 backdrop-filter: blur(8px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(8px);
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-category-badge i{font-size: 11px;
 opacity: 0.9;}
.sie-field-hero__title{font-size: clamp(30px, 5vw, 54px);
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #ffffff;
 margin: 0 0 14px;
 line-height: 1.1;
 letter-spacing: -0.02em;
 max-width: auto;}
.sie-field-hero__tagline{font-size: clamp(15px, 2vw, 18px);
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 margin: 0 0 28px;
 max-width: auto;
 line-height: 1.55;
 font-weight: 400;}
.sie-field-hero__actions{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 12px;
 margin-top: 4px;}
.sie-field-hero__cta{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 8px;
 padding: 12px 24px;
 background: #1E56B0;
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 6px;
 text-decoration: none;
 transition: background 0.2s;
 white-space: nowrap;}
.sie-field-hero__cta:hover{background: #163e82;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__cta--secondary{background: transparent;
 border: 2px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6);}
.sie-field-hero__cta--secondary:hover{background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 border-color: #fff;}
.sie-field-body{max-width: 1200px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px 80px;}
.sie-field-highlights{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 0;
 background: #f0f4fb;
 border: 1px solid #d4e0f5;
 border-radius: 12px;
 margin: 32px 0 40px;
 overflow: hidden;}
.sie-field-intro-block{margin: 0 0 48px;}
.sie-field-intro-block p{font-size: 17px;
 line-height: 1.78;
 color: #374151;
 margin: 0;

<h1 class="title-h1 eac-page-title">Conference on the Future of Europe : the future is in your hands</h1>
<span><span>sandoel</span></span>
<span><time datetime="2021-12-07T08:55:30+01:00" title="Tuesday, December 7, 2021 - 08:55">Tue, 12/07/2021 - 08:55</time>
</span>
<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>
</div>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

<p>Follow on Twitter at&nbsp;</p>

<item>
  <title>European Student Card Initiative at EAIE 2026 in Glasgow - main highlights</title>
  <link>https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/european-student-card-initiative/news/european-student-card-initiative-at-eaie-2026-in-glasgow-main-highlights</link>
  <description>
<h1 class="title-h1 eac-page-title">European Student Card Initiative at EAIE 2026 in Glasgow - main highlights</h1>
<span><span>holbobe</span></span>
<span><time datetime="2026-09-30T09:11:45+02:00" title="Wednesday, September 30, 2026 - 09:11">Wed, 09/30/2026 - 09:11</time>
</span>
<div class="ecl"><p>EAIE 2026 took place from 8 to 11 September, with this year’s theme being “The Rhythm of Revolution”. ESCI featured in five activities: two sessions in the main conference programme and three mini-sessions at the European Commission stand.</p><h2>Shaping the next phase of the ESCI</h2><p>The session “What’s next for the European Student Card Initiative?” brought together Victor Aguilar Mendez from the European Commission, Harpa Sif Arnarsdóttir from RANNIS and Sergi Martínez Rigol from the University of Barcelona to discuss the roadmap beyond 2027.</p><p>The discussion highlighted three main points:</p><ul><li data-list-item-id="ec04a08fab5a0a15faf6d0537ff166c1e"><strong>Build on strong foundations</strong>. Participants welcomed the ambition to further simplify student mobility and emphasised the importance of building on the progress already achieved. They also noted that digital transformation involves more than technical connections, requiring aligned processes, staff capacity and resources.</li><li data-list-item-id="ec8f6683d0b4c64c36760e88ede263ada"><strong>Give institutions clarity and time to prepare</strong>. Participants highlighted the value of clear information on the <a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/european-student-card-initiative/about/esci-2028-2034/continuity-and-preparation?">future scope of ESCI+</a>, practical implications and transition arrangements. The European Commission indicated that 2028 and 2029 are envisaged as transition years.</li><li data-list-item-id="e8a2629faf233a9053a3e7c84c25e2248"><strong>Broaden engagement beyond international relations and IT teams</strong>. Participants highlighted the value of involving university leadership, national authorities, governance bodies and research and education networks.</li></ul><h2>Practical exchange at the European Commission stand</h2><p>Three mini-sessions created space for practical discussion and peer exchange at the European Commission stand:</p><ul><li data-list-item-id="ea46800eaa0963f636bf8742a636fe844"><strong>Digital Officers and ESCI Champions</strong>: “Meet and Greet” explored different opportunities for close collaboration and participants discussed faster communication channels, technical sub-groups and ways to strengthen the community of practitioners.</li><li data-list-item-id="e722608eb7be29071793748afb04db370"><strong>ESCI+ timeline: what to expect and when</strong>, focused on preparations in 2026 and plans for 2027. Participants asked for timely communication, hands-on training, transition arrangements and support to integrate future developments with existing systems.</li><li data-list-item-id="e4abeb75d22c4e87d628dd3a9174bdc0a"><strong>How to issue your first European Student Card</strong> introduced the practical tools available to card issuers, including the ESC Router and the ESC Service Manager for listing services available to ESC holders.</li></ul><h2>Poster session: “The European Student Card: Bridging borders for students”</h2><p>The poster attracted strong interest, with ESCI representatives Elodie Ham (EACEA) and Deborah Arnold (NTT DATA) engaging with participants on the ESCI components and discussing the implications of the ESCI+ timeline with those already involved in the initiative as well as with potential newcomers.</p><h2>Session by ESCI Champions: “Erasmus Without Paper: Getting on board with the digitisation of Erasmus+"&nbsp;</h2></div>
<div class="ecl-u-type-bold ecl-u-mb-m">Intro Text</div><div class="eac-hero"><p>We joined more than 7,300 international education professionals from over 100 countries in Glasgow to discuss what comes next for the European Student Card Initiative and share practical guidance with institutions.</p></div>
  <div>
    <div>Card image</div>
              <div>
<figure class="media-image">
    
            <div class="media-image--main">
            <div class="media-image--enlarge" aria-hidden="true">
                <a class="media-image--enlarge-link" href="#">
                    <i class="fa fa-expand media-image--enlarge-icon"></i>
                    <span class="media-image--enlarge-label">Enlarge</span>
                </a>
            </div>
            
                            <div class="field field--name-field-media-image field--type-image field--label-hidden field__item test">  <img loading="lazy" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/styles/oe_theme_medium_no_crop/public/2026-09/eaie-26-presentation.jpeg?itok=JSRs1Txp" width="991" height="743" alt="The ESCI team presents at EAIE conference, Glasgow">


</div>
            
                            <div class="media-image media-image--copyright media-image--copyright__visible">
                    
                            <div class="field field--name-field-media-copyright field--type-string field--label-hidden field__item test">© European Union, 2026</div>
            
                </div>
                    </div>
                    <figcaption class="media-image--caption">
                
                            <div class="field field--name-field-media-caption field--type-string-long field--label-hidden field__item test">From left to right - Harpa Sif Arnarsdóttir (RANNIS), Sergi Martínez Rigol (University of Barcelona) and Victor Aguilar Mendez (European Commission). </div>
            
            </figcaption>
            </figure>
</div>
          </div>
                        <div id="paragraph-8349" class="lc-padding-top-default lc-padding-bottom-half lc-background-color-white lc-contained lc-stripe-width">
            <div class="slider-text-wrapp ecl-container right-align">
                                            <div class="slider-text-body eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text">
            <div><p>In addition to the sessions organised by the European Commission, <a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/european-student-card-initiative/community/esci-champions?">ESCI Champions</a> (Kristin Anderson, University of Galway, Ireland, Katherine Bruun Funch, University of Copenhagen , Denmark, and Dana Rocklin, Stockholm University, Sweden) ran a practical workshop entitled "Erasmus Without Paper: Getting on board with the digitisation of Erasmus+". The session was very well-attended and enabled participants to share good practices and challenges in using different mobility management systems, including the EWP Dashboard.</p></div>
        </div>
                    <div class="stripe-hero-header img stripe-hero-header__with-slider">
                                    <div class="swiper-slide">
                        <div class="stripe-hero-header--image">
                            <img src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/styles/eac_ratio_16_9_large/public/2026-09/eaie-26-champs.jpeg?h=71976bb4&amp;itok=DbDA6Hfc" alt>
                                                            <span class="slider-text-copyright">
                                   Image: European Commission, 2026
                                </span>
                                                    </div>
                    </div>
                            </div>
            

            </div>
        </div>
    
          


  
<div class="lc-padding-top-half lc-padding-bottom-half lc-background-color-white lc-contained eac-stripe eac-stripe--bg-white" id="paragraph-8350">  <div class="eac-stripe__inner">            <div class="full-html-body">
  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2>Looking ahead</h2><p>Preparation for ESCI+ will continue in close dialogue with all stakeholders via support and user training planned for 2027, helping institutions build on existing progress and prepare for the next phase at a sustainable pace.</p><p>The discussions in Glasgow demonstrated a shared commitment to making student mobility simpler, more connected and more accessible. The next steps will focus on supporting higher education institutions as they continue this work.</p></div>
</div>

        </div></div>
  
          


  
<div class="lc-padding-top-half lc-padding-bottom-default lc-background-color-white lc-contained p-link-group eac-stripe eac-stripe--bg-white" id="paragraph-8347">  <div class="eac-stripe__inner">            <div class="p-link-group--wrapper">
          <div class="p-link-group--title">
            <h3 class="title-h3">
              Related links
            </h3>
          </div>
          <div>
                        <a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/european-student-card-initiative/about/esci-2028-2034/continuity-and-preparation" title="How ESCI is ensuring continuity while preparing for the future" class="eac-link-block">
            <section class="p-link-group--media-eac-link-description">

                        </div>
                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__RECTORS_Q1.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
</div>

                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has a strategy and an overarching structure supporting internationalisation</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The internationalisation strategy is available and prominently displayed on your website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Internationalisation is an important driver for institutional change, and has a great influence on the major activities of a higher education institution (HEI) i.e. education and research. The importance of internationalisation is recognised, and most institutions have a strategy for internationalisation. However, for a strategy to be efficient, and for it to drive the HEI's activities regarding internationalisation, there is a need for its acceptance from across the whole institution. In addition the strategy could also be accessible to external collaborative partners. It is highly important to have the institution's internationalisation and modernisation strategy published and easily accessible to all.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The institution has a clear plan to implement the strategy</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The strategy and policy should include explicit allocation of responsibilities for its efficient implementation to individuals at all levels of the institution, from senior management to the heads of departments, schools and faculties, to academic and administrative staff. This will ensure acceptance and accountability for the strategy. The internationalisation strategy and policy should outline a specific implementation plan that sets out explicitly the financial and human resources available.&nbsp; For example, it is recommended to set up an International Relations Office (IRO) to implement mobility and other international projects.</p><p>As with any other activity, the institutional implementation of the internationalisation strategy is dependent on the people behind the activities. It is highly important for an institution to have staff with the right set of skills and knowledge driving the internationalisation agenda and liaising with international students and staff members. Therefore understanding the development needs of the staff and supporting their professional development should be a high priority for the institution. Such development should focus on both staff engaged in international activities as well as the supporting staff, ensuring the most efficient implementation of international activities and cooperative projects across the institution. For example, trainings/webinars/projects could be organised on intercultural competences and communication, project management, enhancement of internationalisation at home/intercultural, or other activities suggested by the staff and supported by the hierarchy.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Mobility is important to the development of the institution as a whole as well as for the individual participants. Therefore the HEI should make mobility and international cooperation a central element in its institutional policies, and explicitly and consistently promote and support student and staff mobility. Non-discrimination policies and further emphasis on the promotion of mobility for under-represented groups should also form an integral part of the institutional support structures.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes engagement in European and international cooperation projects</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution's internationalisation strategy and policy should explicitly and consistently promote the development of cooperation with partners in other EU and non-EU countries. The activities and co-operation projects agreed by the HEI should be based on identified needs. In addition they should identify geographical and subject priorities of the internationalisation strategy.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The implementation of the strategic plan is monitored</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>International activity, including co-operation projects and mobility should be carefully monitored. Clear and unambiguous monitoring of such activity are key to ensuring success. Explicit indicators should be developed to show specific success scenarios. The indicators should be SMART.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Incentives are provided to staff involved in international activities</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Participation in such international projects should be seen as an important aspect of the professional development of the staff and of the modernisation of the HEI. It should, therefore, be considered a key component in staff evaluation. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels to encourage and recognise staff participating in such projects, as well as allow adequate time to carry out this work.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-case">
                                                <h3>Case studies</h3>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/the-effective-management-and-ownership-of-erasmus-for-internationalisation" target="_blank">The effective management and ownership of Erasmus +’ for ‘internationalisation’</a></div>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/internationalisation-at-the-university-of-helsinki" target="_blank">Internationalisation at the University of Helsinki </a></div>
                                             </div>

                </div>
            </div>

                        </div>
                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__OFFICERS_Q2.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
</div>

                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has established a framework of Inter-Institutional Agreements for Erasmus+ mobility</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on areas of mutual interest</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is vital that Inter-Institutional Agreements are based on areas of mutual interest. These agreements should identify shared quality requirements specific to the planned exchanges, including concrete proposals as to how these activities will contribute to the development of learning and teaching in participating institutions. The involvement of academic staff is key to ensuring that the selection of partners is based on sufficient knowledge of the area. Each HEI should decide who is responsible for initiating, signing and implementing these agreements and the list of responsible persons should be available on the website for contact and consultation purposes.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on the compatibility of study programmes</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Inter-Institutional Agreements should be based on a comprehensive understanding of the partner HEIs, the compatibility of study programmes, quality levels and standards considered adequate for student and staff mobility activities. For example, selected partners should have learning, teaching and assessment procedures that can be accepted by the sending institution without requiring mobile students to do any additional work or take examinations upon returning from the receiving institution. The compatibility of the programmes should be reflected in the learning outcomes to be achieved.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                            </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-case">
                                                <h3>Case studies</h3>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/establishing-a-framework-of-inter-institutional-agreements-for-international-erasmus-mobility" target="_blank">Establishing a framework of Inter-Institutional Agreements for international Erasmus+ mobility</a></div>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/inter-institutional-agreements" target="_blank">Inter-Institutional Agreements</a></div>
                                             </div>
                    <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close-text"><i class="fa fa-times fa-2x"></i><span>Close</span></div>
                </div>
            </div>
                         <div class="eche-report-full-question-wrapper">
                <div class="eche-officer-question-title-wrapper">
                    <div class="eche-report-title-icons-wrapper">
                                                 <div class="eche-report-officer-number">
                            <img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/eche-pdf/number-corner-orange-3.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">

                            <div class="eche-report-officer-number-text">3</div>
                        </div>
                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__OFFICERS_Q3.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
</div>
                    </div>
                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution expresses its commitment to equal access and opportunities to mobile participants</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">There are specific provisions e.g. in the general policies, rules and regulations of the institution</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>In signing the Erasmus Charter for Higher Education, the institution agrees to respect <strong>in full</strong> the principles of non-discrimination as set out in the Programme. The institution must clearly demonstrate through its policies, rules and regulations that equal access and opportunities to mobile participants from all backgrounds. Which means that all individuals or groups will be treated equally, irrespective of their characteristics. In accordance with Article 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, there should be no discrimination "based on sex, race, colour, ethnic or social origin, genetic features, language, religion or belief, political or any other opinion, membership of a national minority, property, birth, disability, age or sexual orientation". For more information, see: <a href="http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf">http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf</a></p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The principle - that extra fees are not being charged to incoming mobile students - is implemented</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The receiving institution must <strong>not </strong>charge any type of fees to incoming mobility students for the tuition, registration or examination of these students or for their access to laboratory, library and other facilities offered to local students.<br>In certain cases, however, mobile students may be required to pay small fees for insurance, student unions, use of miscellaneous materials (e.g. photocopies, laboratory products) on the same basis as these are charged to local students. Students should be made aware of these extra costs before the start of mobility. Fees may only be charged in the case of full degree mobility or for students registered in joint degree programmes.&nbsp;</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">All students and staff (incoming and outgoing) are treated equally in all academic and service matters</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>In accordance with equal access and opportunities, all students and staff should be treated equally in all academic and service matters. Clear appeal procedures should be in place to ensure equal treatment.                         <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The purpose of the Learning Agreement is to provide a transparent and efficient preparation of the study period abroad and to ensure that the student will receive recognition in his/her degree for the educational components or traineeship successfully completed abroad.                          <p>To ensure effective staff mobility, it has to be based on a signed mobility agreement. The mobility agreement has to acceptable and signed by all parties in advance. There are four key elements set out by the mobility agreement, which are intended to increase the relevance and potential impact of the mobility. These are:</p><ul><li>The overall objectives and academic rationale of the mobility,</li><li>The institutional requirements or strategy, and the mobility's added value in the context of modernisation and internationalisation,</li><li>The activities or teaching programme content to be undertaken by the staff member, and,</li><li>The expected outcomes and impact of the mobility on the professional development of the staff member at both institutions.</li></ul><p>For this to work effectively, there needs to be dialogue and discussion between the three parties prior to the signing of the mobility agreement having agreed the common goals which are acceptable.&nbsp;</p>                      </div>

        <h2 class="eche-report-section-title eche-pdf-page-break">During the mobility</h2>
        <div class="eche-report-section-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-report-full-question-wrapper">
                <div class="eche-officer-question-title-wrapper">
                    <div class="eche-report-title-icons-wrapper">
                                                 <div class="eche-report-officer-number">
                            <img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/eche-pdf/number-corner-orange-10.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">

                            <div class="eche-report-officer-number-text">10</div>
                        </div>
                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__OFFICERS_Q10.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
</div>
                    </div>
                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question"> During the mobility, your institution fosters the integration of the incoming mobile participants</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The institution appoints responsible person(s) to deal with practical issues (e.g. social, health, and/or psychological problems)</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution should ensure there are named, visible persons who are responsible for the practical issues associated with integrating mobile students. This visibility should be ensured through introduction to this function during the Welcome / Orientation period and be detailed on the website so all mobile students can easily access this support, throughout their stay.&nbsp;</p><p>Non-academic mentoring and support arrangements should already be outlined in the Course Catalogue of the receiving HEI, in the section on general information for students, with relevant contact persons in the respective areas. Academic advisors should have close contact with the practical services which are available to incoming participants as they are often the first line of contact to the incoming student. Further information sessions should be arranged for all staff who work with incoming students to ensure they are adequately signposted on to the appropriate services they require.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It appoints responsible person(s) to deal with academic issues (course timetables, student attendance, coursework, relationship with academic staff, etc.)</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is important that the receiving institution appoints specific named academic advisors who are responsible for dealing with problems related to academic issues (course timetables, student attendance, coursework, relationship with academic staff, etc.) of incoming students.&nbsp; Information on mentoring for thesis writing for incoming students is particularly important and clear mentoring arrangements should be agreed upon between the student, sending and receiving institutions and organised before the mobility.</p><p>For traineeships, a mentor, different from the supervisor, should be nominated to support and encourage the mobile student while in the receiving organisation. The mentor should also provide information on the culture of the enterprise and informal codes and conducts, of the receiving organisation. The contact details of both the supervisor and the mentor should be specified in the Learning Agreement.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It organises Welcome / Orientation activities at the beginning of each semester</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>An important aspect of the support arrangement is the welcome or orientation activities. These welcome / orientation activities should provide the incoming students with the necessary information on practical and administrative arrangements, to allow incoming students to meet local and other mobile students, to introduce the learning and teaching methods of the receiving institution, academic regulations, the institutional culture, health and safety issues. These activities should address any type of concern of the incoming student, and reduce any psychological pressure they might feel during their first contacts at the receiving institution. The welcome&nbsp; / orientation activities should be designed to take into account any cultural and religious sensitivities of the incoming students (ensuring a range of activities to suit different types of students).</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It organises activities to integrate them in the receiving institution and the local community, e.g. with the support of student organisations, Erasmus+ Student and Alumni Association etc.</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>As well as academic and practical support from the institution, incoming students need to feel fully integrated into the student community, something which is best done by their fellow students / peers. Local student association(s), such as Erasmus Student Network (ESN) and the other associations’ member of the ESAA - Erasmus+ Student and Alumni Association (<a href="http://esaa-eu.org/">http://esaa-eu.org/</a>), play an important role in supporting incoming students. Incoming students need to feel welcomed and included in the student organisations. To help this process, the student organisations need to be aware of their role in supporting this integration and have access to the right resources, information, guidance and incentives. As institutions often have many types of student organisations, cooperation between them is encouraged through meetings together, social activities and buddy programmes. A key aspect of these activities is to make sure they are for all students so incoming students are integrated with the local students and hence the culture. Student organisations include for example, ESN (Erasmus Student Network) or ESAA - Erasmus+ Student and Alumni Association (<a href="http://esaa-eu.org/">http://esaa-eu.org/</a>). ESAA runs a buddy system to encourage integration of incoming students with their peers inside the institution and share good practice with other member associations around Europe.</p>                      </div>
